Tattrp. _ . THE LITTLE GIRL OF THE "FREES AIR FUND."

'Twas little she knew of the sweet green grass, With its wonderful wealth of clover, Which, far outside of the city's walls, Was spreading the broad fields over. Yet blue her eyes as the summer skies, And as sunny her tangled hair As the goldenest sunbeam ever sent To lie on the earth so fair. What wonder she opened her blue eves wide When she learned, one happy day, That she and many a child beside ' Were to travel far away " To the fairy place where daises grew, And the streets were soft and green," And her little heart o'erldowed for joy Of the glad things yet unseen. Old Farmer Jones on the platform stood When the train came in at last, And the little " waif " who was sent to him ' He clasped in his strong arms fast. " F.u. it's never a chick nor a child have I," Said he to the agent then, I And just as true as the heavens are blue, Fit be good to this gal. Amen !" An I he bore her home to the shady farm. And he "turned her out to grass," • AS he merrily said. And the sun and breeze Made free with the little lass, And kissed her cheeks till they blushed as red As the reddest rose that grew, And innocent mischief peeped from out The once sad eyes of blue. . Dear friend," says a letter from Farmer Jones, " Ther's no two ways about it, This farm's got used to the wee gal's laugh, An', in fact, can't thrive without it. Why, bless your soul it would do ye good To watch the chick each day A-turnin' the old place upside down • Along of her happy play. " An' me an' my wife we don't see how There's anything else to do But just hold on to the leetle gal, If it's all the same to von. An' I reckon the blessed child that lives With the angels in the skies Won't mind if little new one stays To wipe the tears from our eyes. "An' the mother this EP, al has lost will find My pet in the angel land, An' I make no doubt but they'll both be glad As they watch us hand in hand. So, now, whatever there is to do, Just write it for me to sign, An' God's blessin' rest on the 'Fresh Air Fund,' Your work as well as mine." —Leeds Mercury Weekly.
MARY D. BRINE.

In all cases of heartache, the application of another troan's disappointment draws out the pain and allays the irritation.—Lytton. Sorrow commonly comes on horseback, but goes away on foot.—Adam. You may know an old bachelor by the fact that he always speaks of a baby as "it." Give sorrow words; the grief that does not speak Whispers the oyerfraught heart, and bids it break. —Shakespeare. Walking down St. James's-street, Lord Chelmsford was accosted by a stranger, who exclaimed, "Mr. Birch, I believe?" "If you believe that you will believe any- thin:r." replied the ex-Chancellor as he passed on." Rusticus wrote a letter to his love, And filled it full of warm and keen desire; He hoped to raise a flame, and so he did— The lady put his nonsense in the fire. "Pray, my lord," said a gentleman to a late respected and rather whimsical judge, "what is the difference between law and equity courts ? " "Very little in the end," replied his lordship ; " they only differ as far as time is concerned. At common law, you are done for at once; in equity, you are not so easily disposed of. The former is a bullet, which is instantaneously and charm- ingly effective; the latter is an angler's hook, which plays with its victim before it kills it. The one is prus- 'sic acid, the other laudanum." Many years ago, when a Berwick election petition was being heard before a Committee of the House of Com- mons, considerable amusement was caused by the diffi- culties of the South-country Members to make out the Berwick dialect. "Well." said counsel to a witness, "where did go?" "He went wi' we," replied the native of the ancient borough. "Wi' we?" repeated the puzzled Chairman; " what is wi' we?'" " Well," came the reply,'he went wi' we—he went wi' huz." " Huz ! But who is huz ?' " 6" fluz' is we !" cried the Borderer, indignant that his tongue should be so little understood. A young American lawyer, employed to defend a cul- prit charged with stealing a pig, resolved to convince the court that he was born to shine. Accordingly he proceeded to deliver the following brilliant exordium : "-May it please the court, and gentlemen of the jury, while Europe is bathed in blood; while classic Greece is struggling for her rights and liberties and trampling the unhallowed altars of the bearded infidels to dust; while America shines forth the brightest orb in the poli- tical sky—l, with due diffidence, rise to defend the cause of this humble hog-thief." BUTTERINE AND MARGARINE.—The name butterine

given to a compound of fats is nonsensical, and was in- vente I only to deceive the poor. But to give the name of mlrgarine to such compound is also incorrect. The composition of all vegetal oils and all animal fats con- sists chiefly of oleine (composed of oleic acid and glyce- rine), margarine (composed of margaric acid and glyce- rine), and stearine (composed of stearic acid and glycerine), in various proportions. By boiling with steam, compressing, and by distilling by steam, oleic acid and glycerine are separated, and the compound of margaric acid and stearic acid is made into candles. Pure margarine cannot be extracted except by costly manipulations in the laboratory, and is not an article of trade. _

American tourists abroad, as we have seen in several I well-known instances, do not always carry with them intense feelings of reverence for what they go to see. , S unetimes this is rather painful to sensitive souls, and I sometimes it is very amusing. Two or three summers I ago I was in a railway train going down through Italy and we had just reached the point where the branch line strikes off for Rome. I was looking out at the window, lazily contemplating the sign "A Napoli," which was I over the other side of the station, when a voice, with all the fine nasal resonance of the most vigorous of our Yankee brakemen, rang out through the train r— "Na-a-ples Junction! Pahsengers for East Rome and Rome Centre change cars here !" The peal of laughter , that followed showed me that I had many compatriots in the other carriages. Everybody took the joke. ANIMALS THAT LAUGH AND CRT.—We have several , curious stories of animals that laugh, as related by the ! keeper of a museum and menagerie. He says :—You wouldn't think a great, big, clumsy creature like an elephant could manifest emotional weakness;i but be can, and what's more he often does. 'I here was Colum- bus. Years ago he went stark crazy. He tore 'round ! like mad, and smashed everything as though he were ' tussling with so much paper. Before he could kill any- body the building was cleared of the people and the , doors locked. For three days he had the place to him- self, spending his fury on the cages and animals. At last I we trapped him in ropes and chains suspended through the skylights. The chaining process brought him to his senses at once, and what was our surprise to see him go Into something like a hysterical fit. He moaned piteously, as a person will frequently when suffering some great mental -torture, the noise occasionally swelling into a roar. His huge ears flapped to and fro rapidly, and for two hours and more a perfect stream of tears poured from his eyes. These manifestations even continued after he was released frOm the irons, showing they came from sorrow and not anger. Columbus was more than an ordinarily intelligent elephant, and seemed to realise the brutal havoc he had spread during his temporary insanity. Here is another singular thing—the Cingalese elephants always weep in captivity. No, Columbus wasn't a Cingalese. Another time he accidentally knocked a small boy down who got too near while he was sweeping his trunk around for confections. He pretty near scared the urchin to death by picking him up and putting him on his feet. I rushed at him with tile hook, but there was no necessity for a reprimand. The tears were running from hi % eyes, and he absolutely appeared to be penitent. The boy had been feeding him , with sweetmeats. Elephants will always cry when ' mortified or disappointed. NORTH limernroDow Et.scrrion —Both candidates have now issued their addresses. Mr. Saunders recognises 83 a fundamental principle of Liberalism that man has certain national rights, approves of free education and manhood suffrage, and enumerates a long list of reforms which meet with his support; but declares that they must all wait until we have doce justice to our Irish fellow subjects. Mr. Ail wyn Fellowes is in favour of allotments and a compre- hensive system of county government, but declines to be a party to handing over 2,000,000 of our countrymen in Ire- land to the tyranny of Mr. Parnell and his American asso- ciates. The Liberals are holding meetings in every part of the division, the speakers on Tuesday night including Messrs Mahoney, Power, and Halley Stewart, ME'.',. The Conservatives opened the campaign on Tuesday evening, when Mr Marriott, M.P., spoke at St. Ives. Both parties express themselves sanguine of oneness. The Conservative majcrity at the last election was 365; but the Liberals claim to have made a slight gain in the registration since then.

to Warrington and Wigan. The first stoppage after leaving Runcorn was Halton Castle, distant about three and a half miles from the former place. Standing on a very high rock, the site, while rather difficult to reach, com- mands a grand and far-reaching view in all direc- tions. Unfortunately, the amenities of the place were greatly lessened by a heavy shower which commenced to fall before the party arrived, and continued till after their departure, dimming the prospect very considerably. But for the presence of a considerable number of residential buildings surrounding it and located on the( accessible side of the slope, with a small hotel partly built on the site, the castle, now in ruins, Fight_prove a very dreary scene to all but antiquarian enterprise. THE CASS CAPE: PROSICI7TION OF ENDACOTT.—On Tuesday, at Bow•street, before Mr. Vaughan, Police Con- stable Endacott appeared to answer a summons taken out against him by Miss Cass charging him with wilful and corrupt perjury in connection with the evidence given by him against Isar on the 29th June at the Marlborough-street Police Court, when he proceeded against her for soliciting prostitution in R•gent•street. Mr. J. P. Grain and Mr. F. M. Abrahams (instructed by Mr. J. A. Bartrum) prosecuted, and Mr. St. John Wontner appeared for Endacott. There was a considerable manifestation of popular interest in the case, and, as is usual on such occasions, the doors of the court were beselged by crowds of curious persons anxious to get places inside from which to watch the proceedings. Soon after half-past one o'clock Mr. Vaughan came on to the Bench, and the defendant Endacott at Ones took the place below the dock in which persons answering summonses are usually accommodated. He was well dressed in civilian attire. He has a strong, well-knit frame, but his face shows that the events of the last few weeks have worn him down' and generally unsettled him. He listened patiently to the evideocv, and until the rising of the court, at about twenty- five minutes to six o'clock, gave no sign of outward emo• tion. The prosecutrix, Miss Cass, is a somewhat slightly- built young woman, of medium height, with dark hair and eves, and a pale complexion. Police Constable Endacott pleaded not guilty. Mr. J. P. Grain read over the evidence given by the defendant at the Marlborough-street Police Court, on which the charge was based, and stated Miss Cass's case. Miss Cass, Madame Bowman, and Mr. Edgar Wslford, who witnessed the arrest, gave evidence. Tbe court afterwards adjourned until Friday.

It would not have been possible for Hyacinth to hide from her mother—even if she had sought to do so— so much, at least, as the purport of what had passed between her and Vincent Lorraine. Mrs. DesmOnd wopid naturally ask what bad detained the girl so much later than she had intended to return home, and Hyacinth would as soon commit a crime as tell an untruth. Besides her face would show her mother that something had occurred to trouble her. The poor child would have given the world to escape utter- ing a word on the subject, but the ordeal must be gone through, and it was no use to shrink from the in. evitatle.

Mrs. Desmond was standing at the gate when Hyacinth came up; and it was almost dark; but the mother only said quietly, "You are late, dear," and the girl, without a word, followed her into the house. 'Tea is ready, dear," said Mrs. Desmond, but Hyacinth shook her head. "I can't touch anything," she said, flinging down her hat. Mrs. Desmond looked at her, sat down in the low arm-chair which she usually occupied, and stretched out her hand—" Come here mavourneen."_
Hyacinth went forward, knelt by her 'natter's side, and hid her face on her knee.

"My child !" said the mother, trembling, and laying her hand on the soft curls. I know that you have met Vincent Lorraine to-day. Tell me what passed." Then brokenly—not once looking up--giving only the substance of the truth. Hyacinth told her tale ; but breathed not a word of the parting moments—that clasp—that kiss; those words that rang in her ears with a strange sweetness only half comprehended. In silence Mrs. Desmond listened, and when she spoke it was with resolute calm.

" Hyacinth, this man is even worse than I had be- lieved him: He loves you ; but were promises regarding the future carried out, I slioui, ,er forgive his past—no, my child, not even if yon loved him, for with all his dazzling qualities, he could not make you happy. I could not trust you to a man who has wasted his life in dissipation, and I scarcely know how he dres to ask yorr love; still km to ask you to trust to him to teach you the lesson you have not yet learned. It is a strange beginning to such teaching to shew you, and desire you to follow that example, how little he cares for the most sacred ties. Ile certainly would not scruple at any means to gain his end." Hyacinth knew what her mother was thinking of. hut she whisperrl, "lie could not, mother; there is no one here who would aid him."

"No, my child, but he may find means elsewhere. Understand me, Hyacinth. What I mean is this—l think that Lorraine will wait a little; perhaps try to persuade you to dope with him—he knows well he could not gain my cOnsent to his wishes; and, failing your yielding to his persuasion, he will not hesitate to use force, to the extent of imprisoning you at Curra- more fora day or two; thinking that by that time you would believe your good name injured, and so consent to be his wife."

" Mother !" The girl lifted her head, and her black eyes burned like living fire. "Vincent Lorraine knows me too well to dream of that ;: he knows that I would rather brave all the world could say than sacrifice my life to a man, whom, even if I had Toyed, I. should hate then for such a deed. And, mother; he would not, he could could not dream of such villainy !" But Mrs. Desmond thought she could better gange Lorraine's character than her (laughter, and fell into a mistake. She misjudged Lorraine's. intellect, and in- deed, hiihonour also. Roué the man might be; but he was utterly incapable of seeking to gain his end by such cowardly terrorism, and had he been, he could not have fallen into the mistake of supposing that a strong- willed, high-spirited girl like Hyacinth could be frightened into submission by the phantom of the world's opinion. But the girl kept in her heart her own thought—shrinking, she hardly knew why, from uttering it; and it ditil not seem to occur to Mrs. Des- mond. Bride Desmond was certainly no match for Mr. Vincent Lorraine, and Hyacinth, who could have. helped her, was something very fike a traitor in the cam p. Mrs. Desmond had only looked in her child's- flushed face while Hyacinth thus equally defended Lorraine's astuteness and morale, and shook her head a little sadly, but as Hyacinth rose; she added, "I shall be compelled to leave this place. Mr. Loreaine is severe on the lawlessness of tenant farmers; but he has him- self clone more than they have to restore the anarchy of the Middle Ages." " Leave here !" Hyacinth started, and recoiled. Then a sudden light sprang into her face, which her mother, watching her, misread. If they left Bally- goyle—then Lorraine would follow—would seek her (Hyacinth), end,. so he would be safe. The girl breathed more freely. "But there is no need, mother," she said, turning 1.0 the door. " No need yet—not just yet ; but there may be soon."

Hyacinth made no reply to this, but went slowly oat of the room and sought her own, and there she knelt down again, and covered her face, and tried to think. Heart and brain were in a tumult. Had she been wrong after all? had she been unjust to Vincent Lor- raine in turning a deaf ear to his prayer? Was he right when he said he was more to her than she had dreamed of? She. travelled over all the incidents of the time since she had known Lorraine; and her throbbing heart, amid passionate sobs, half joy, half grief, gave back only one answer. "Your heart would be further from me than it is if I had ivooed 'you as other men woo," Lorraine had said; and now—now she owned the truth of thoae words. Even when she was most angry with him she was not farthest from yieldine• to his influence. Wh.:.• did she not hate him—scorn him, for that last daring act that was almost insult; those words that, had other lips uttered them, she would never have forgiven ? Yet there was no scorn—no hatred—in the young face lifted for a moment to the soft moonlight that strearned.into the chamber, and hidden again, the sensitive woman nature shrinking from that light as though it could pierce her soul and read its secret—scarcely yet fully acknowledged to herself. That night, while Hyacinth lay sleepless, Mrs. Desmond wrote a letter to Vincent Lorraine, and sent it early the next morning. Hyacinth appeared at breakfast; indeed, she was in the garden, gathering the usual summer bouquet for the table, when her mother came in. 'Mrs. Desmond did not speak of Lorraine, but she •-ked that Nellie had called last evening and said IL. I:racy was going to Dublin in a few days. Hyacinth coloured painfully, and her eyes filled y/ith tears; but she made no reply. What could she say? She was glad that Terence O'Conor called in the course of the morning, and she went out riding with him. He thought her wilder than ever; she laughed, jested, ran mod races, and seemed in reckless spirits. The day was sultry, and two or three times Terence complained of the heat, but Hyacinth always revelled in heat, and when Terence said there was a thunderstorm brewing, and he believed the electricity was infhienciug her, she said with mock gravity, "Am I so mad, then? I sup- pose it is the electricity." On the way homewards the riders passed Regan's holding. The man was in the front garden of his cot- tage, digging, but he looked up and sainted respectfully as Terence and his young companion 4proached. O'Conor would have passed with a simple response to Regan's "Top o' the maiming, yet anner, an' Miss Hyacinth," but the girl drew rein. She generally stopped and talked to all the people ; she had a special motive now in talking with Lorraine's tenants. Her quick eye had noted, too, that. Regan was planting flowers—she had seen that some way off,—and she saw that as the man paused, leaning on his spade, he so placed it as to partly conceal the little plant he had been inserting in the ground. "Why, Regan," said the girl, carelessly, "are you planting flowers?" "Sorts a bit, missy," replied Regan, with the readi- ness of his nation. "What'll I be puttin' flowers' in for when 1.11 be turned out in a few days? I was just diggin' up a few, missy, to take away wid me. I sup- pose Misther Lorraine won't grudge me a few plants that cost scarce anything?" "Sure no; but it would be better to pay the rent, 1 think, and then you need not go." Regan shook his head gloomily. "I can't do It, missy; but Misther Lorraine's hard, and won't believe me."

"He wasn't hard to Doolan's widow, Regan," intes7i posed Terrence. -. Regan, shrugged his shoulders, and was silent. He could not very well deny this fact; but he was not going to speak a good word for his landlord. "What about the weather, Regan?" said Hyacinth, coming to the rescue. "Mr. O'Conor will have it there will be a storm to-night." Regan looked up quickly—glanced over the sky, and his glance as it travelled downwards rested for half a second on the towers of Curramore, visible from this spot. He shook his head. .-. _ _

"No, mis:sy," he said, cheerfully, "there'll be ne storm to-night., 'twill be moonlight.' As he spoke, hc stooped, picked up a little bunch of displaced weeds, and flung them aside; but the insignificant action was another link, to Hyacinth's keen, watchful intelligence. She noticed the look at• Curramore, that might well have escaped an experienced detective, and the dis- crepancy between the tone of Regan's reply and his action in throwing away the weed, gave her an im- portant clue. He spoke lightly—cheerfully; but the weed he did not cast away carelessly, as became a mere idle action; he almost flung it down; his fierce, im- patient thought found relief in the act; the cheerful- ness was the mask. Then the planting of the flowers seemed to argue a feeling of security hardly consistent with. the shrewdness of Regan's character; for the man well knew that Lorraine would employ 'force to carry out his will. This was wllat Hyacinth read: "I can plant safely, for Mr. Lorraine, will not live to disturb me. We want a night of storm, or at least darkness, for our work. To-night will Mat do—it will be moon- light. Curse it !" • "Well, Regan, I hope it will be moonlight," she said brightly. ".Good morning." And the riders went on; and all the while on the homeward road, the girl's heart was sick with the terror of the future. The fell schenie was terribly near its fulfilment; yet that brave heart did not faint. She would yet discover the plan and foil it—she, this tender atripling—this girl of eighteen, who had a man's strength ot mind with all a woman's—and an Irish- woman's—winning tenderness. She was certain that the scheme—whatever it was—which had been hatch- ing ever since the day when Dermot Grady fired—as he believed—at Lorraine anti missed, had its head- quarters at that worthy's farm. Grady was the leading man among the tenants—the best off in worldly matters, and his premises were better salted for secret meetings than those of many of the others; for there were barns and outbuildings almost hidden from the house; and Ilyacintli.knew that Mrs. Grady, though willing to shut her eyes, and pass by things she was not compelled to see, would not countenance meet- ings in her house which could bear no other complexion than conspiracy. At Grady's the girl might obtain some clue, without which it was useless to warn Lor- raine. her-mind was made up before she reached the Wood Cottage. Quick in thought, fearless in action, subtle in wit, they must be cunning and powerful who foiled Hyacinth Desmond. If to-morrow threatened a night of storm, to-morrow afternoon she would go to Grady's farm. She must save Vincent Lorraine, come what may; she had watched to this end when she did not know how dear he was to her, and now—now—if Mil befall. him ;—it would be the signing of her own death warrant.
(To be eon:hilted.)

div.p: A LUCKY FARTHQUAKE.

For more than half a century, Georgina Countess of Gaddaway had been one of the ornaments of English society. The early days of the fourth William saw her a bride, a reigning beauty. The Victorian Jubilee, thanks to the progress made by those artistes who study the pre- servation and decoration of the human form divine, be I held her apparently not the worse for wear. Ban then it must be recollected that the memories of those who ' remembered her as a bride had grown somewhat hazy. In any case, if not exactly a thing of beauty (the present Earl's wife called her an old mummy),Lady G. was cer- tainly a joy for ever. She was full of spirits # even to giddiness, and the presence of "Fluffy," as her Mends called her, was eagerly sought for at London, dinner- tables and country-house gatherings. Lady Gaddaway had survived her husband by a longer lapse of years than she cared to enumerate. She was, undoubtedly, an old lady, but wonderfully well preserved. Of all her youtlifik passions she retained but two; her love of society, and bar hatred of some of her connections, principally the wife of the present Earl, whose baptismal name was Maria, but who, before her marriage, had been better known as Baby Briggs, of the Nudity Theatre. This latter, Georgina Lady Gaddaway hated with all the concentrated venom of a long life spent in a society not remarkable for its charity. Not that "Fluffy" was a particularly spiteful old lady, but she could not forgive the present Countess her extreme youth. That is a fault a woman never pardons in another. Perhaps it was this one good fiery hatred, combined with the one great love of her life, which kept Lady Gaddaway's blood stirring and active, and allowed her to rattle about all over Europe and the British Isles, from one social entertainment to another, always up to every- thing and ready for everything. Her horizons had changed. Grandchildren occupied the place of her hosts of fifty years ago; but, like the Brook or the Wandering Jew, Lady Gaddaway went on for ever. The state of preservation of Edmond About's colonel with the broken ear was nothing to hers, after an even longer period. Next—after a succession of idolised pug-dogs, who died regularly of apoplexy, were wildly bemourned, and. then replaced the following week—Lady Gaddaway loved her nephew, Lord Glenarragh. He was really her great-nephew, but nobody except Debrett dare call him so to Lady Gaddaway. She loved him for his good looks, his I wildneQs, and his fun; he had been able to wheedle money I out of her ever since he was in knickerbockers. Even in the days of the Kilkenny cats the Glenarragh barony had been a poor one. In less remote times, thanks-to Mr. Parnell and the Land League, its financial position had not improved. But for his aunt's help, Glenarragh would not have known how to get along at all. It was an open secret that he was to be the heir to her own property, and to the savings she had made out of the handsome jointure charged on the Gaddaway estate, over which three successive Earls had grumbled in vain. Now, if there was a point on which Lady Gaddaway was a shade behind the age, it was in regard to, the modern melte of plutocracy. She liked money well enough but she hated it new. The Baby Briggs business had given her a horror of misalliances. Therefore all her ac- quaintance at Cannes, whither she had flitted in. Fela- ruary, like every one else who could get away, were amazed to find she had taken up the Potiphar, Higgs. But the astute old lady knew what she was about. She had discovered the Higgs, an unknown mine of wealth, hovering aimlessly enough along the Riviera, fresh from their native wilds of Buffalo. Lady Gaddaway having made sure of the wealth bequeathed by the late. Mr. Potiphar Higgs to his only daughter, promptly proceeded to exploiter them. "Pm very much obliged to you, my dear Duchess," said "Fluffy," shaking her fuzzy front at that lady, as she bade her good night. The Duchess's great ball at her Cannes villa would not be over for many hours to come, but Lady Gaddaway couldn't keep the hours she once did. "I'm very much obliged to you for having had them to-night. The girl's very handsome, and shell do very nicely for Glenarragh." But she wouldn't have been quite so sure of it if she could have seen her dear nephew at that moment. It was the night of the Hunt Ball at Snaftleborongh. That great function was the last of three dances which were wont annually to convulse Wessex society over a period of about ten days. Lord Glenarragh had been staying at a house near for all three, and had made. such good use of his time that he had fallen in love with, and , actually proposed to, the youngest and loveliest of the five daughters of a local squire, who was as hard hit by the agricultural depression as, he '(Glenarragh) was by the Land League. The lovers were sitting out in a draughty passage of the Corn Exchange, where the Hunt Ball was held, watching the sea of pink coats and white dresses surg- ing beyond the doorway. • Arid must you really go ?" she was asking. "I don't see how I can get out of it. You don't know what my aunt is. She's evidently set her heart on my coming to her for the Shrove Tuesday ball." "Will it be such a good one—better than this 2" "I don't know anything about it, or who gives it, and I don't want to. I shall just hate it." But perhaps you'll meet someone you'll think nice 7', (archly.) But this latter suggestion Glennarragh promply and satisfactorily refuted. Three days later the train de luxe had borne him southwards to meet Lady Gaddaway at Nice, in time for the last day of the Carnival saturnalia. "Fluffy" was in great spirits. Royalty, who had run down for his annual lark, had been most affable to her, laughing enor- mously at one or two stories the old lady had collected for his especial benefit. Her nephew was hardly in such good form. He suf- fered himself to be dragged like a lamb to the slaughter to the Princess de Plafond's ball, and all unsuspiciously danced with the fair Higgs. Lady Gaddaway liked her nephew to be attentive to her, but she could have par- doned him that night if he had not shown such a desire to escort her back to her hotel, when she left imme- diately after supper. If he had been much struck, she argued, he wouldn't have wanted to come away. But she determined to sound him. "Well, Glen, and what do you think of her ? " asked his aunt, when they were back in the salon. Glenarragh was pouring out a whisky and soda absently, his thoughts far away. "Think of her? Why, she's charm—" Then he recol- lected himself. " Think of whom, aunt Georgie?" "Why, boy, are you blind? The beauty, Miss Potiphar Higgs!' "What, that American girl you introduced me to? By Jove! she is a rum un, quite an aboriginal! Told me she'd never lived in the country till she came to Nice— comes from a city, Buffalo; asked me if I was only a lord, and not going to grow into anything more. I in-
A manufactory at Poiut Pleasant, Wandsworth, belong- ing to Messrs. Hamilton and Co., manufacturing chemists, was on Wednesday destroyed by fire, together with its con- tents.

At a meeting on Monday of the Pomeroy and Castle Caulfield Orangemen, resolutions condemning the action of the Rev. Thomas Ellis, and confidence in Mr.. Russell, M.P. were unanimously adopted. Shortly after 11 a.m pn Tuesday Knell House, Seven- oaks, the seat of Lord Sackville, took tire. The stables and barns adjoining where the fire originated were quickly con- sumed, 200 tons of hay being destroyed. formed her I'd done growing some time, and that as for the title, we'd found that goqd enough for the last eight or nine centuries. But, auntie," coming and sitting down on the eofa by Lady Gaddaway, and continuing per- suasively, "let's drop that and talk seriously if we can. ' I've got a piece of news for you." Now, one of Lady Gaddaway's maxims in life, one of her favourite recipes for the preservation of youth and beauty, was that you should never lose your temper. But on this occasion, when her nephew imparted to her the fact of his engagement, she was so incensed that she threw every consideration of her appearance to the winds, and made up for years of abstinence by a regular ' explosion of wrath. Half an hour later the two parted, Lady Gaddaway declaring that she would never set eyes on him again, and would leave every farthing she pos- sessed to Baby Briggs' son and heir. Glennarragh went to sleep, feeling about as uncom- fortable as it was possible for a young fellow of his light- hearted temperament to feel. He awoke suddenly more uncomfortable still. His bed was being rocked from side to side like a boat in a sea, and the china and the furni- ture were falling about the room. Though his experience I in such matters was limited, it did not need a second's reflection to convince him that there was an earth- quake. It did not take him many seconds more to robe himself classically with a blanket, in a manner which, though it would have become him admirably had he been sitting for his portrait as a young Roman patrician, was hardly`adapted for a chilly morn- ing on the Riviera at seven o'clock. Then he fled with the panic-stricken, tiiiaintly-garbed crowd, who surged down the hotel stairs and into the garden. The first persons he saw there were Lady Gaddaway's English footman, looking like an acrobat, in crimson breeches and white shirt, and her French maid in curl papers and very little else, wringing her hands. ! mon Dieu! Madame its Comtesse, est-elle eneezelie ? She come not! She is killed!" Then Lord Glenarragh realised that his aunt was still in the hotel. He rushed upstairs again, over masses of debris of ceiling and walls which encumbered the stairs and passages. The door of the salon was jammed; with some difficulty he forced it open, and brought an avalanche of plaster about his ears. The quarrel was all forgotten in the great and appal- ling emergeney. He never recollected that he was not to speak to her again. "Aunt Georgia! aunt Georgie ! where are you? Come out—come down—there's not a moment to be lost ! " An agonised voice from the bedroom: "I can't, rsan't, Glen! I can't And my things !" IV Confound your things, aunt! The house'll be down about your ears. Come, come !" "I can't come like this, I'd sooner die! I cant find I

Lord Glenarragh waited for n 6 more. He filing open the door and rushed in. He stopped short at a sight the like of which no man or woman (except the French maid) had ever beheld. Then he fancied he must have come into the wrong room. This could never be his aunt. But the voice was hers.
---- "Go away, go away, Glen, there's a dear boy; leave me.to die I I'd much rather—"

But Glenarragh was equal to the occasion. lie seized a blanket from the bed, and, enveloping Lady Gaddaway bodily, bore her triumphantly down-stairs, and &posited her, mummy-like, on a garden-seat. Presently a choked voice issued from the folds of the blanket:
" Glenarragh, bend your head down; I want to wills- rr something." He dig as..he was bidden.
"My darling boy, you may marry whom you like, and give you half my income and leave you everything, if you'll only go back into the hotel and fetch my—my hair and my teeth." _ .

When, five minutes later, Glenarragh returned from an expedition of some danger, bearing the artieles in question, and also a large white umbrella which he opened and put over Lady Gaddaway's prostrate form,. he felt that he had won his bride as chivalrously as any knight of old.

A LANKYSHER SONG. Tho Cockneys scorn t' Lankysher lingo, An t' ruff twang ut's spokken t' North, Thers a deol o' good sense lyin hidden Along t' stuff as they think little worth. An they'd find t' "porridge vters " wur Christians, If they heard a sweet music tit tongue Re-echo ear sentiments, blood warm fro th' heart,. In a gradely good Lankysher song. We've Waugh, an Ben Brierley, an Healey, Sam Laycock, an two or three mooar, Who sing, i' th' owd twang, strains o' Poesy, As glorifies th' ruff rooads o' t' poor. Yo'll hear ther sweet lilts sung i' t' meadows, Wheer Luv tells id tale, t' fleawrs among, An bi th' fireside, o' dark fleets i' winter, Thers mony a good Lankysher song. When fagged eawt an weary wi labour, Them magic as leetens yor looad, In a jingle as catches yor fancy, An geds to yor heart th' nearest rooad. Then flashes on t' mind mony a pictur, As memory reawnd Life's chambers hung, For Comfort an Hope—close linked blessins— Often beam fro a Lankysher song. For rousin up owd recollections 0' th' time when we knew nowt at o Abeawt this world's sorrows an troubles, An played wi owd mates hi t' skoo wo ; For bringin to mind th' gentle voices As warned us fro every wrong, Mekkin tears show heaw mon loves his parents— liowt at o licks a Lankysher song. When Nature spreads beauty o reawnd us, On t' moorlands, an valleys, an hills; An th' hedges are speckled wi blossoms, An sunbeams lie clustered on t' rills. Thers mony a heart, gladdend wi t' glories 0' th' owd country loynes, far fro t' throng, As feels id deep gratitude shapin idsel Into t' words ov a Lankysher song. Do yo want sumtnat simple an hooamly, I' measures uts leetsum an gay. To bring thowts o' gradely enjoyments Yo've joined in i' times past away? Or 'let surnmat hooarnspun an gammy, A bit ov a wheeze ?—nod too long— Toll find t' stuff as meks faces broaden wi mirth,, In a reet-deawn good Lanitysher song. Then here's to th owd "time honoured" keawnty, As teks t' leead i th annals o' trade, To id blunt spokken sons an fair dowters,— May they o be content, an weel paid! For th lasses are t' bonniest i England, An th lads are bowd, fearless, an strong; An th deeds as hes proved em as equals to t' best,. Gleam i' mony a Lankysher song. Here's to t' fooak as is plain an streyt forrud, As'll co a spade nowt but a spade, I' th owd rude Anglo Saxon, as Fashion Tries to mend,—Hoo's a tongue scrapin jade! Tho we're twitted o'er unpolished manners, An snubbed thro eawr "barbarous tongue," We've t' laff on eater side, for we know English. weel, Beside th " twang " ov a Lankysher song. Jacx o Ames.

THE BULGARIAN SITUATION: PRINCE FERDINAND'S JOURNEY AND PRO-

MISWRITE, SAVGIIDAY EVENING. —Prince Ferdinand, accompanied by 'the Regents and all the Ministers, ar- rived here at half4past twelve o'clock this L..ternoan, and was received with cheers by the crowds which were as- sembled on the quay. On landing his Highness was presented with !bread and salt 'by the Mayor, who also delivered an address, to which 'the Prince replied in the Bulgarian language. Several 'other deputations ad- dressed the Trine°, welcoming him as the Saviour of tulgaria, each speech being ',followed by loud cheers. 'Prince Ferdinand, attended +by a brilliant suite, then pro- ceeded to the house specially prepared for him, the route to which was lined by troops. Later on his Highness was entertained at a luncheon by the Municipality in the public gardens, when several loyal toasts were pro- posed, the Prince replying in Bulgarian. During the progress of the banquet Colonel Nikivoroff, the corn- mandaat of the Sobirmla garrison, gave a toast expressing the fidelity and devotion of the army to the Prinoeund to the independence of Bulgaria. '"We will I cover tie Balkans with 'corpses," said the commandant enthiMiastically, " rather than allow the entrance of enemies into the Principality." After the 'banquet the military officers chaired Prince Ferdinand amidst the enthusiastic acclamations of those assembled, and the Prince subsequently reviewed the troops of the garrison, and•then left for 'Tirnova. Vntrore, MONEAT.—Details have been 'received this morning from rwriera, respecting the taking of the oath as Prince of Bulgaria on Sunday by Prince Ferdinand of Cleburg The ceremony was of great solemnity, and was marked by remarkable enthusiasm and 'unanimity on the part of those present The oath was administered by the Metropelitan of Widdin, who exhorted his High- ness to maintain the Constitution and fight for the inde- pendence of 11111ga-rift. None of' the foreign diplomatic *gents or consuls were present, and the proceedings, 'lncluding the :reading of Prince 'Ferdinand's proclama- tion, were itttended by manifestations of unbounded loyalty and affection to the new prince. With a view to allaying useless regrets for the hero of Shonitza, the por- trait of Prince Alexander. which bangs in the hall of the I Grand Sobrarife, was veiled during the ceremonial.

AMERICA.—THE RAILWAY DISASTER— "THE 'FISIIING 'DIFFICULTY.

NEW Wax, !FRIDAY Nrear:—Latest particulars re- garding The terrible accident in Illinois state that 155 dead bodies have been identified, but it is added that this number does not represent the total loss of life. The evidence given at the inquest tends to support the theory that the bridge Wa.S parposely set on fire with a view teetrbbery. Many of the deaths are due to the want of surgiehl aid and to rough liardling in the attempt to rescue the victims. A physician who reached the scene soon after late accident says—When I arrived I found the geeatest confusion. Hell -itself, could not present a more -horeible picture. Men and women were fight- ing with3sisath and , ready to eclutch at a straw to get saved. One man held (lie dead wife and a dead little child in- hic arms, while his own-feet were broken and propped-tin- the wreck. I relieve&the unfortunate man of his burden, and helped to drag hissi out and bring him to a sleerrine carriage. One of thewreatest misfortunes was the fact t hat the wreck occurred in a place almost a desert. It ,v.as impossibile to give sufficient assistance. There were, no ambulances—nothing to carry them in. They were Shagged and pushed, andsthis accounts for a great number of people who succumbed to their pain." The superirstendent of the &Sway says that the more he has inveet:gated the more clearly,it appears to him that the bridge was set on fire. He bar; observed many thieves-at work, and stopped them while despoiling the wreck of property and money. The citizens say that a gang of suepisious fellows had been hanging about Chatsworth for some days. Many of these were found early at the wtecir, paying more attention to relieving • the bodiez, of valuables than caring for them otherwise. PRILADELMIK, SATURDAY.—florrible details of the Chatsworth railway disaster fill the newspapers. The • number of deadihus far ascertained is 153. The Illinois - Railway Commission has gone to Chatsworth in order to hold an investigation. The claims for deathseceasioned, with those for damages on account of injurieseustained, • already threatened against the ToCede, Peoria, and Western Railway amount to nearly $1,0e0,000. The . company has just emerged from bankruptcy. The phy- .siciarts say-that la& of care for the wounded led to an increase in the number of deaths. The railway officials endeavour-to-show that the trestle bridge was fired by Anis:meant& who desised to rob the train, but the testi- .trionY received indicates that the structure was ignited by a prairie or some other accidental fire, which, owieg Whack of supervision, the officials failed to discover. The bridge was inspected on Wednesday afternoon, but -there was no inspection between five o'clock and mid- alight when the disaster occurred. General removals .of•the dead and wounded are being made from Chats. I worth. The railway was not cleared of the wreck till -tosiday. NEW Yonx, MONDAT.—Tho Iftrald publishes an Ottawa 'telegram, stating that a traveller from Boctouche, a small svillage on the St. Lawrence, reported that a week ago a Canadian cruiser fired into an American fishing -vessel, off Boctouche, bringing down her mast, and ,causing her to capsize. The crew, numbering 15, were drowned. New YGRIC, MONDAY.—The Canadian steamers Hast- ings and Kathleen have been seized bv the American Customs officials at Charlotte, New York State, not having been inspected by the Uaited States inspectors. They were afterwards released. ANOTHER liatt,wAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. PHILADELPHIA. WEDNESDAY. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad express train from the West, on arriving at Wash- ington this morning, ran off the line at the station, owing to the fact that the air brakes worked badly, and was wrecked. The driver and two passengers were killed and 15 persons were badly injured TIrE RELIEF OF EMIN BEY.

ZANZIBAR, SUNDAY.—It is announced here that the mes- aengers sent from this place by the British and Italian Consuls to inform Emin Bey of the dispatch of a relief expedition under Mr. Stanley arrived in the beginning of May at Mika, a place situated on the eastern coast of the Albert Nyanza, after they had been for a long time detained bv Kussiki, King of Unyanyembi, and by Mwang,a, King of Uganda. If these messe.ngcrs were able to find means of crossing the Albert Nyanza in order to reach Mhagi, a station on the west (oast of the lake, and one of ten stations still held by Emin Bey and Signor Casati. the camp of Emin should have received information of Mr. Stanley's attempt at the end of May. It was stated at Mlisa that at the beginning of May Emin was in the Umjaro district in good health, and en route to Lake Muta Nzige by way of Kakibbi.
SEVENTY THOUSAND DEATHS FROM
CHOLERA.

Rolm FRIDAY.—The cholera epidemic is now confined to Sicily. SIMLA, MONDAY.—Medical returns from the north-west provinces show that 70,000 persons died there from cholera during Juno and July, being 1 per cent, of the population.
1,000 HOUSES DESTROYED BY FIRE. CONSTANTINOPLF, SUNDAY.—A great fire is raging at Scutari, several hundred houses have already been burnt down.

CONSTANTINOPLE. MONDAY.—The fire it Scutari was got under this morning, but not until 1,000 houses, two churches—one Greek and the other Armenian—bad been destroyed. Two women and one child perished in the flames, and an immense number of people have been rendered homeless. The Sultan has given orders that the same committee which was formed to relieve sufferers from the recent fire at Arnautkoi shall take measures for succouring the unfortunate people affected by this fresh disaster. His Majesty has himself sent a sum of £(T)3,000 from his priv.-/ purse.

div.head: ATTEMPT TO ,BLOW UP A RAILWAY BRIDGE.
div.p: ATTEMPT TO ,BLOW UP A RAILWAY BRIDGE.

On Monda,y night or early on Tuesday morning, a de- termined attempt was made to blow up the second bridge on the West Clare Railway, which spans the I ?ergus at Lifford. about two miles from Ennis. Four =dynamite cartridges had been placed on the surface of •the bridge, which is a solid iron structure, on cut stone ers. Two of them exploded, but did very little damage. s,ad caused no injury to the permanent way. Two other cartridges, with detonators, that had not exploded, were found on the bridge, with•fuse attached. A later telegram says the attempted destruction of the bridge seems to be traceable to purely local enmity. Placards, boycotting the railway on account of the un- popularity of one of the chief officials, have been postod throughout the counts; .and:it is probably in connection with this that the outraste was attempted.

A lad, named John France, died at Leigh, Lancashire, on Thursday, from hydrophobia. A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office at 2-30 p.m. on Thursday. to discuss the state of public busi- ness. LII the Ministers were present except Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. me nemara agents at Queenstown nave recervea telegram Announcing the arrival at New York on Satur- day at noon of the Etruria, which left Queenstown on Sunday week. The passage was made in the short time of six clays, three hours and a half. This is the Etruria's best performance, and equals the Umbria's fastest record. FATAL POISONING CASE. —A strange case of poisoning occurred at Luton on Sunday night. Samuel J. Alger, aged 65, foreman at Messrs. Brown and Green's foundry, ate some tinned oysters from a can opened the previous day, and was soon afterwards seized with illness. Dr. W. Tonison was called, but the man .grew wcrse, and 'died between tight and nine o'clock. On Sunday the congregation in St. Peter's Church, Bolton, were in the morning without a clergy- man. The bells were ringing but information was con- ,veyed to the wardens that the Vicar, the Rev. J. R. Coghlan, had been taken suddenly ill and was unable to preach. Under these circumstanefu the bells were etopped. No service was held, and the congregation ze- ta/stied b'eme.

It is alleged that Hutchin- son gave birth to a chikl, of which Chadwick was the father, and that he secretly buried its body in the garden. An inquest has been held on the body, and the jury found that death wart caused by negtect. THE FIRE AT WHlTELuir's.--The adjourned inquiry into the cause of the death of the four men who were killed daring the fire at Whiteley's establishment in London was was held on Wednesday. Farther evidence having been given, the jury retired, and after a short consultation the Foreman announced that they had resolved to Aek the Coroner to adjourn the inquest until the 24th October. ' They thought that the evidence submitted pointed to the theory that the fire had been wilfully caused by tome person or persons well acquainted with the building, and that tbe circumstances called for a OeverAntent inquiry, The inqueet was accordingly adjourned.

The (length, of the swing girder wilt be 289 feet, with a clear width of opening span of 140 feet. The ttain con- veying specially invited guests :arrived on !the :scene just before one. These inide their way ,to the stand that had been erected, running eat into the -river, anti here they were almost immediately after joined ~,by Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. Mrs. thadstotie having Vestry whistle, and Mr. Gladstone waved a Stag, the cylinder on the Cheshire side of the Dee slowly descended ,into its position, amidst deafening clieers from the ~ponple on both banks and those in boats 'Me ceremony having concluded. _

Mr. GLADSTONE proceeded to address the company on the platform. lie said the deed he had performed .ents.a symbol and commemoration of the operation :of the greatest importance; mid, on behalf of the whole Intel& of North Wales, he thanked Sir Edward Watkin and his coadjutors for having taken the action they had, with a view to more closely uniting the two countries. ;EXECUTION OF THE CREWE MUR- DERER-C9.NPESSION OF THE CULPRIT,

—.—. Thomas Henry Bevan, 20 years of age, was executed at Enutsford Gaol. Cheshire, on Tuesday morning, for the murder of his aunt, Sarah Griffiths, at Crewe. in March last. The prisoner, while spending a day at his aunt's house, managed to steal her purse, containing 17s. fid., and being caught in the act, he knocked her down with a dolly-peg, and kicked her to death. His little half-sister entered the house at the moment of the murder, and Bevan made a brutal assault on her, also.leaving her insensible When arrested, the culprit displayed the utmost caHousness, and while in gaol pending his trial he seemed very anxious to know what sort of fare persons condemned to death got. When told they could order anything they liked, he said he would 'make the prison ;iutborities keep him well be- tween the time of his conviction and execution. This dout, however, but took the ordi- nary per Latterly he became very penitent. ea, h prison not ft er carry. and told the whole story of his crime to the deputy- governor.and the prison chaplain. Acting on his direc- tions,th,oofficials went, to Crewe and found the stolen purse, with. tt)(3 money untouched, concealed under a hedge, precisely as the prisoner described. His half- sister made a sensation at the trial by asserting that a Mrs. Parsons 'entered the house .cluring the murder, and exclaimed.' Stop it. Mister: you'll kill her." Mrs. Par- sons denied this at the time, and the prisoner, in his reve- lations, said Mrs. Parsons never entered the house. He had an interview with six relatives on Saturday, and expressed deep penitence. On Sunday he partook of Holy Communion for the last time, and onMonday he wrote eight letters to relatives, which he directed to be posted after the execution. At night he went to ttel at a quarter-past eleven, slept soundly till 5 30 a.m on Tuesday, and took breakfast an hour later. He bade farewell to the warders in an unfaltering voice, and, with- out uttering another word, walked to the scaffold with a firm step. Berry was the executioner, and, as the prisoner was a very light-made youth, weighing only Sat. gibs., he was given a drop of six feet. Bevan died without a struggle, death being, to all appearance. instantaneous Only the officials and five reporters vrera present at the execution. The culprit had made a full and detailed confession of his crime to the murdered woman's sister. He admitted that he murdered the old woman in order to get her money, and stated that the little girl, Mary Tones, hie half-sister, returned to the house before the woman was dead. He tried to strangle her, and afterwards he went into the room where the old woman lay on the floor and jumped upon her body many times. This bears out the testimony of the doctor who examined the woman, and who declared that all her ribs were broken. Bevan then possessed himself of her purse, which contained about 155., and then left the house. He begged in a written statement that Mr. Griffiths, the murdered woman's husband, an old man nearly would forgive him.

WRECK ON THE HIGH SEAS: TERRIBLE SUFFERINGS.-- The White Star liner Britannic. which arrived at Queens- town, on Thursday morning, from New York, brought in- telligence of the loss of the vessel Sara, and a great portion of her crew, between San Pedro and Martinez, California. The Sara was struck suddenly by a heavy surf, and cap- sized. All aboard perished except the captain and a few of the sailors, who saved_ themselves by clinging to the bottom of the vessel. Five of the sailors became crazy, saving they were going ashore, and immediately plunged into the sea. They had no sooner touched the water than sharks devoured them. The captain, a sailor, and a small boy were the only survivors. They clung to the wreck, on which they re- mained for eight dam experiencing fearful ;privation and suffering.

The Prince of Wales arrived at Homburg on Sunday evening, and immediately paid a visit to the Germiui Empress. The employment of boy clerks and boy copyists in the public departments is greatly on the increase. Twenty- seven boy copyists have been appointed during the week, and the total for last year was 160. Charles Kynaston, farmer, was charged at Shrewsbury, on Monday, with the murder of his wife, by shooting her, on August Ist. The Bench dismissed the case, but the prisoner stands charged with wilful murder on the coroner's warrant

inssaAxcnisEmrisr or. 2,000 C ROFTERS.—ft has pin transpired that clO4O upon 2,000 crofters in the Western Isles are disfranchised by not, having paid their poor rates before the statutory period. The island of Barra is totally disfranchised. The number on the roll at the last election was 220, and the number now returned as disqualified is 227, being seven more than on the roll in 1885. In South Uistthe nutober disqualified 15464, being 141 less than were enrollod at the last election. In North lust. the number enrolled in 1885 was 336, and the number disqualified 74. In Harris the number on the roll is 274, and of these 109 are disqualified. In the Long Islands the total number disqualified is 874, out of a total of 1,435, the number enrolled in 1885. The total number enrolled for the Islands is 3,570, and there are disfran- chised 1,500. It, is stated that the other islands and West Coast Highlands are in a similar position.

The Right Hon. George Joacinin Goschen, M.P., Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, who was born on August 10th, 1331,has just completed his 56th year. Two large 50-ton cannon have just been sent from the Oboukoff works at St. Petersburg to the Black Sea for the ironclad Catherine IL, launched last spring. A fire broke out on Monday in a tenement house in Sheriff-street, Dublin. Joseph Taylor, a clerk in the Dublin and Glasgow Steam Company's office, was burnt to death. The Queen has signified her intention of conferring the honour of knighthood upon Mr. C. J. Pearson (Procurator of the Church of Scotland) and Mr. H. M'Andrew (Pro- vost of Inverness. . .

Mr. Horatio Mansfield, deputy stipendiary magistrate for Liverpool, died suddenly, at his residence in that city on Saturday. The deceased gentleman had officiated as deputy magistrate for between 10 and 12 years. Three inhabitants of Varengeville have been sentenced by the Dieppe magistrates to six months' imprisonment for stripping jewelry from the bodies of victims of the disaster which happened to the Victoria. The bodies were washed ashore near the village. One of the prisoners is a woman. Harvest operations are in full swing in Nor,thamptes- shire, Cambridgeshire, and Hunts. The Hessian fly has been reported in each county. There are good crops of wheat, and millers report a fair yield. Barley is good. but oats are hardly an average, whilst beans and root crops are a partial failure. After many weeks' cessation, rain fell for several hours over north Wales on Saturday. The drought had become so serious that work had been suspended for some days in many of the industrial districts, and hundreds of hands were thrown out of employment. The river Dee, it is said, has not been so low for 19 years. FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.-111C premises of the Standard Tea Company, 559, Battersea Park-road, London, kept by Mr. Martin,were dest..‘yed by fire early on Sunday morn- ing. All the inmates were saved with the exception of a servant girl, name unknown, aged about 17, daughter of a publican at Guildford. Considerable damage was also done to adjoining premises.

_ FATAL FALL DOWN A QOARRY,—VVIIOO the OWM went to work at Mrs. Parr's rand quarry, Greetby 11111, Orms- kirk, on Saturday, they found the body of a man named James Campbell, aged 46 years. It appears that the de- ceased was at a beerhouse in Ormskirk until eleven p.m. on Friday, at. which time he started for home. It is supposed that he was crossing the land where the quarry is situated for a short cut to his house, but owing to the darkness missed his footing and fell down the quarry, a distance of 36ft. A WELSH CtorraNsaistc—lt is announced that Mrs. Francis, a widow residing on the Welsh hills at Tymaen Pyle, has attained the exceptionally advanced ace of 107 years, being born on the 15th August, 1780. The aged lady, who looks remarkably well, is, it is stated, very hale, and can thread her needle without using her glasses. She moves about with ease, and is enableertA) attend to domestic duties. Mrs. Francis is at this period of the year the object of great interest, to tourists, with whom she converses freely.

CRITSIZED TO MATTI INT • WMILD COLLIIDt7. inquest was held at ltryn, near Wigan, on Saturday. on the body of Thos. Rogers, 26, who met with a shocking death at Messrs. Crippins', Bryn Hall Colliery, on Wed- nesday. The deceased was working with another man, when a large block of coal suddenly fell upon him, crushing him to the ground. The poor fellow's cries for help were soon answered. but as his comrades were extricating him the roof again fell, completely burying and crushing him to death. Thomas Pierce, who was assisting, was also caught, and seriously in- jured. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

COLLISION AND LOSS OF SIMERAL LINW IN TON ENOT.ISII en ANNEL-The Greek stearner,AntircaVagn i an o,was towed into Plymouth Sound, on Saturdav,in a stoking condition, having been in collision on Friday off the Eddystone, with the commercial steamship Norbiton, from Cardiff, with coal from Rouen. The l4;orniton was struck with such tremendous force that. she began to settle down rapidly, and there was no time to save four of the crew and the mate's wife and children, who all went down with her. The Andrea .Vagniano picked up the boat containing the remainder of the crew, and tried to make for Plymouth. She had, however, been so seriously damaged that she could do very little, tier fore compart- ment being full of water. She kept afloat until day- break, and was then pieced up by a Plymouth tug, and docked in safety on Satarday afternoon.

, A SINGULAR 1118CC)VRRY.—An old man, named Isaac Praddle, who follows the calling of a shoehlack in Pear- street, Leiceater Square. 11,ondon, was evicted from a cellar at 49, Charino, Cross Road, on Saturday. When a warrant officer frorn"Marlborough-street Police Court and the landlord attempted to remove some bags, boxes, and pails from underneath a dilapidated bedstead, the man and his niece, who, like himself, appeared to be poverty- stricken, refused to allow them to be touched. The boxes and pails were, however, ultimately brought out from under the bed, and were found to be full of money, over. which dirty sacking had been nailed. One box alone was so heavy, being filled with from four to five hundred- wei§lit of coppers, that it took two men to carry it. Some of the bags contained silver and gold, literally coated with dirt and verdigris. The miser stated that the money was the result of 40 years' accumulation.

" BIIND Tom."—ln the civil Courts of Baltimore judg- went has been given in the action brought on behalf of Thomas Wiggins, better known as "Blind Torn," a negro pianist of considerable repute in the United States. The order of the Court is that General James N. Bethune, who has kept Blind Torn in his possession since the days of slavery, shall deliver him to the United States Marshal on August 16, at Alexandria, Virginia, and that the Marshal shall deliver him safely into the hands of Eliza Bethune Who was appointed Tom's committee by the Supreme Court of New York; and also that General Bethune pay over $7,000 to the order of Court, for the credit of Blind Torn as his earnings. There is another suit pending against John G. Bethune for $lOO,OOO. Eliza Bethune, the present committee, was appointed at the request of Charity Wiggins, the mother of Blind Tom, who insti- tutied the suit against the &ghillies about two years ago to' recover the possession of her son and for the earnings of his concerts which General Bethune had received since 1865. SEVERE FROST TN AVOOST.--POTATOES BLIGHTED.— Throughout Lancashire a very keen frost was ex- perienced during the early hours of Sunday morning, and the consequence is considerable damage to potatoes, especially on light and moss lands. On Farington Moss as well as Leyland Moss many farmers will be serious losers through the blight, for acre upon acre of potatoes yesterday evidenced signs by blackened tops that the growth had been killed. The crops, however, on heavy rich land have sustained comparatively little injury. From Rufford, Ormskirk, and district, similar reports have been received, one farmer alone having sustained irretrievable loss to the extent, of eight acres. Here heavy showers of rain fell on Sunday and during Mon- day morning the result being that harvest operations were impeded throughout the neighbourhood. At Broughton-in-Furness ice, the thickness of a penny, was gathered, and from here accounts have come to hand that a largo area of potatoes was blighted with the frost. The effect of the 'frost on the potatoes will be the more keenly felt., inasmuch as the crop is far from plentiful this year. and on 84turday potatoes were re- tailed at so much as one shilling per score. On question- ing our "oldest inhabitant" as to the visitation of frost during August, we find that it has only been experienced twice within the last 50 years, once 44 years ago, and the other 17 years since. THE GREAT WALL OF CHINA A MYTII:—.Abbe Larrieu, formerly a missionary in China, has published a pamph- let on the Great Wall of- China, to demonstrate that it does not and never has existed. The popular belief is that this wall stretches for about $OO leagues across China, from the sea to the province of Kansu, that it is wholly constructed of cut stone, and 30 cubits high by 12 broad. It is believed to run straight on, regardless of obstacles, going down valleys and up mountains, with- out a break, except such as time has made, along its whole course. This notion originated with a Jesuit named Martini, who visited China about 1650, and his description was followed by subsequent writers. M. Larrieu has lived for several years under what would have been the shadow of ihe Great Wall had there been one: he has studied the writings of recent writers— especially Abbe flue—who have crossed the line of the alleged wall in various places; lie has likewise studied the Chinese history of the subject. and his conclusions are as follow ;—(1) The term 'Great Wall" ia at the bottom of all the misunderstanding, and it comes from the Chinese expression "the wall of the ten thousand li ;" (2) as described by Martini and other writers who have copied him, this wall does not and never did exist (3) a Chinese Emperor undoubtedly diO conceive the idea of a great wall from the gulf of Long on the east to Ransil on the west, and this, though never realised, had a heg,inning; (4) all along the pro- posed line of the wall square towers of earth, or of earth faced with brick, were constructed at considerable dis- tances from each other, but these were never joined together by any wall as was originally intended. In some of the defiles along the route there are walls, but these were intended to close these particular passages, or they are merely the wells of villages, and are not parts of a larger scheme. Hence the only part of the scheme of the Great Wall carried out was the construction of these scattered towers ; the rest never went beyond the brain that conceived it, it, was never more than a fancy, and it is now a myth. This huge Chinese wall. Bays Abbe Larrieu, is a huge Chinese lie, and, as for the million soldiers which were said to guard it night and day, they are myths likewise. . _ .

T. Jacons Om cures rheumatism and neuralgia. TERRIBLE GRINDING BrOmE ACCIDENT.—A terrible ac- cident happened at the foun Iry or Messrs. 0. Pickles and Co., Burnley, shortly before halt-past twelve en Thursday. James Bland, over fifty years of age, was working at a massive grinding stone turned by steam when the stone gave way, and the broken pieces flew in all directions. Bland was dashed to the ceiling and instantly killed. Two of his sons were working there at the time. During the progress ot a nre at the premises us assr eating-house keeper, named Bates, at 51, Old-street, St. Luke's, Shoreditch, early on Monday, the inmates were, , being rescued by means of a ladder, provided by two I constables, when Bates, having seen all the other inmates safely to the ground, was descending the ladder last, with the two policemen, when it broke, precipitating , them 20ft. below. Bates and one constable escaped with slight bruises, but Constable Withers was injured in the back. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT • COTTON MILL—A destructive fire occurred at an early hour on Saturday morning at Messrs. Melland and Cowards' cotton mill, Beaton Mersey. The firm had closed the works and taken out the boiler fires on Friday night in view of the trip of the workpeople on Saturday. A fire was, however, discovered' in the drying-room at midnight. The Stockport The Brigade rendered admirable service, but a large block ot buildings was completely gutted. Several thousand. pounds damage VMS done, hut the lons is largely covered by insurance. The origin of the fire is unknown.

°MOW. REPOAT ON TAN NAVAL MANCEI7VRES.—Arr official report has been issued by the Admiralty on tbe recent naval mamptivres. 'the movements of the several squadrons are detailed at great length, with remarks in passing on each phase of the manceuvres. With refer- ence to the actions of chief interest in which Admirals! Dewitt and Fremantle were engaged, the report states that the attack of Admiral Fremantle's squadron was completely successful at Falmouth, while at the Nor, the defending force had the best of it. Opportunity is taken to deny the statement that Admisal Fremantle was unable to escape into the North Sea, having no, charts. TAB QUEEN AND ROMAN CATROITO NUNS.—Cardinal' Manning has forwarded to the Bishops of London and Rochester, who have undertaken the distribution, the , greater part ef the seven hundred doyen articles of cloth- ing worked by the Roman Catholic nuns of England and presented to the Queen aIS a Jubilee gift, to be sub- sequently distributed among the poor at her Majesty's pleasure. The Queen has expressed to the Cardinal her, gratification at the offering, and asked him to see to its, distribution among the poor, reserving some portion for! poor Roman Catholics. The Cardinal has thought the, best way of carrying out her Majesty's comman ls was to give the clothing to the London poor; and, having' reserved a portion for poor Roman Catholics, he has asked the Bishops of London and Rochester to sec to thei proper distribution of the remainder. Isle of Man, was riding on the switchback rail; way at the Derby Castle Grounds. Douglas. when in try.', big to accelerate the speed of the car he fell off and watt precipitated against one of the harriers with great focal' and killed Instantaneously.— On Monday an inquest was held at Derby Castle ow the body of Edward Landon, clerk in a . land agency office in Cork,: who fell off a ciltehhack railway car in the Castle groueds on Saturday night. LORD ROSEBERY IN MANCHESTER. The Earl of Rosebery, president of the Royal Commission of the Melbourne Centennial Exhibi- tion, was present on Wednesday at a meeting of influential citizens of Manchester in the Town Hall, presided over by the Mayor (Mclennan Harwood). In the course of an address he said that from one point of view it was of very great importance that the men of Manchester should find it in their power and consonant with their inclinations to assist the Exhibition at Melbourne. It was most important, at a time when foreign countries pro- tected themselves against our goods as if they were the Hessian fly or the Colorado beetle, that we should send to our colonies the best specimens of our machinery and our products generally. • To the department of art, also, the Royal Commissioners attached very great importance, for the Australian colonies were very considerable purchasers of pic- tures, and showed an interest in art which was quite beyond the experience of new communities. , He did not know whether any of the gentlemen I present had pictures which they could see their- -1 way to send to the colony of Victoria. but he was sure that if they could the works would find a more appreciative multitude of spectators than in almost any comounity in the world. And, in addition, I ' any little ;tokens of goodwill and helpfulness we might show to 1 at a time when \ the colonists now would be repaid, and helpfulness a ve might wish for all the goodwill I Before concluding' .e could get. a brief visit to Manchester, the k Earl of ROEISBEEY on Wednesday addressed a gathering of the memb ors a the Reform Club 1 has- tilyt convened in the bi."l"-room. His Lordship said he had never knowi ' the Liberal party so all the real elem. , strong in mats of political strength as lat the present moment. . They had only one leader and one principle, and though that principle had separated them from urn on with many with . whom they had worked former iy and with whom i they might yet work again, it w. us a principle of so , Vivifying a character that the pai ty who possessed i I it, even n a minority, was atm. 'ger than many ' majorities. He ridiculed the assi ,rt Salisbury, vie wed in the light of the recent of Lord tions, that the Government had the .- recent elec- vivantage of having received a mandate from the ci * luntry ; and ' with regard to the position of the Liberai Unionists, f lie said that in the moment of triumph a hd of al)" lands to proaching conquest. they held out their i them with greater cordiality than before an d with I the less suspicion of self-interest. The door (.. Liberal party was wide open for them to entei ; to those who did not choose to do so another path open.

GEORGE BALL AND JAMES SHAIV FOR £2O. I A. game of bowls, 101 up, for the championship of Warrington and £lO aside took place on the green attached to the Bull's Head Hotel, Church-street, ! Warrington, on Saturday afternoon, between the above-named players. which was witnessed by upwards of 400 spectators. The green was in first- class order, and both men played a grand game, which was a remarkable one for short runs alter- nately made by either player. Ball has been the local champion for the past 15 years, and has on several occasions beaten some of the best bowlers in Lancashire ; but this is his first match since J. Bromilow, of Westhoughton, easily defeated him at Blackpool last season for £5O aside. Shaw, on the other hand, has been active during the present season, having previously played seven matches and won five, and bids fair to rival his opponent in due time. The above-mentioned green was selected on account of its being a subscription green, and neither player being members, which was best calculated to test their capabilities. Ball was the • first to score, totalling 10 to 5, and 15 to 6. Shaw ; now made two runs, a 8 and 7, reaching 21 to 19, the pair afterwards keeping close together up to 26, when Ball went to the front, scoring 32 to 26, 42 to 35, and 52 to 41. After a short interval, Shaw made a run of four and Ball seven, the latter Iplayer reaching 63 to 48, when he appeared to fall I off his play, and Shaw made a run of 8 and then 01 totalling 65 to his opponent 64. Shaw now went to 76 to 67, 79 to 69, and 87 to 76, when Ball made a 1, grand run of 11—"87 all'—the pair afterwards peeling at 91 and 93. Shaw now made two singles, when Ball made a run of eight, thus winning a well contested and exciting game by six points, the scores being—Ball, 101; Shaw, 95. The game I lasted six hours and a half, the latter portion being ' played almosti aN pin the 2.‘ 1 1111 . j AT BANK QUAY. On Saturday afternoon, the Bank QuaUyASUbscrip- tion Bowling Club green was the scene of a, handi- I cap main of bowls, the pr)prietor (Mr. R. Mellor) j offering a copper kettle to a shilling entrance. The green was in good order, but on account of the I above match there were not many spectators. Forty-four players entered the contest, It. Webster gaining the first prize, copper kettle and 15s; T. Elison, us and a letter rack; Joseph Gleave, Gs ; and R. Miller, W. Lee, and J. T. Massey 4s each. BOWLING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. The members of the bowling club in connection with the Liberal Club recently went to Knutsford, 1 where they played a friendly game of bowls with a local club. The players numbered 24 on each side. I and the game resulted in a win for the Knutsford ; men by 14 points. Subsequently a return match was played on the green at the club in Bewsey- street. The Knutsford club only broudit eleven men, but the Warrington club gave them three I men, and a game of fourteen aside was played. It ended in a win for the Warrington club by 50 ' points After each game a substantial tea was par- taken of, and each side expressed themselves well pleased with the reception given them. An agreement was made that the clubs should meet.. , again next summer.

MR. GLADSTONE had a congenial task, on Tuesday, in performing the ceremony of laying the first cylinder of the new swing railway bridge over the river Dee. The pro- posal to bring North Wales, so to speak, twenty miles nearer Liverpool and the rest of West and South Lancashire is one which has for a long time had his approval. Two years ago he cut the first sod of the Wirral Railway, and on that occasion't as on Tues- day, he referred in forcible and felicitous terms to the enormous advantages which the railway system conferred on the country, and more especially to the gain to North Wales which would result from a score of miles being saved in the transit of goods and passengers. Wales is remarkably rich in minerals; but slate. as Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out at the luncheon which followed I the ceremony, is exceedingly heavy, and as I the price is low it is of the first importance to effect a saving in carriage. Referring to the I possibility of sending milk from North Wales, I Mr. GLADSTONE enunciated a truth which is too little regarded when he said "there is I not an article of more vital interest to the masses of the population." He proceeded to suppoit his assertion by quoting medical authority for the statement that in Glasgow it had been found that ricketts in children was most prevalent when milk was least used. Large cities are not usually well supplied with pure, wholesome milk, and Liverpool is no exception to the rule. If the erection of , this bridge across the Dee should be the !means of largely increasing the supply of milk to Liverpool, it will be a blessing to the commupity which will not be "disguised." The new route will be valuabln, too, in another respect. North Wales presents so many delightful nooks and corners—and its coast is everywhere so charming—that it has become the holiday ground of Lancashire people. The roughs of Sc. Helens have taken to assaulting the police from the house-tops. One constable has been struck with a brick from this coign of vantage, and another with a chimney pot. The offenders have, of course, been sent to gaol, the magistrates intimating that they were determined to deal severely with the men who thus take to the tiles.

Mr. Caine, M.P., says he does not intend to go to Mr. Gladstone until Mr. Gladstone comes to him. Really, ri,•)w, what a liberal Liberal Unionist! Mr. Gladstone will, of course, at once ac in sack-cloth and ashes to this great man of light and leading. The Liberal party could not exist without Mr. Caine.

Mr. Brunner, in the course of a short speech at Runcorn, on Saturday, whilst the polling was progressing, said he was "not only in favour of Horne Rule fcr Ireland, but for England." This is the right note to strike—Home Rule all round, including Scotland and Wales, with an Imperial Par- liament for Imperial affairs, at which each country shall be represented.

The " Morning Post" says : "It is clear that the present machinery of the Unionist party is breaking down, and that repairs are urgently required to obvidte an otherwise in- evitable catastrophe," This is a pretty can- did expression of opinion from a Tory organ. But the difficulty is that the machinery can- not be repaired. The principle on which it is worked is bad, and there is no remedying that.

The " London Times" and some other Tory papers are bewildered by the great success of the Liberal party at the North- wich election. Unable to accept the obvious explanation of the victory—:he growth of Home Rule principles—they have rushed to the conclusion that there hasn't been enough of Coercion, and they advise Lord Salisbiry to proclaim the National League.
