Abhor each other, but when the frith is spanned by a great bridge the abhorrence is at an end. And the bridge across the Dee will be a great one. Its span is to be thirty-six feet larger than that of any other bridge in the United Kingdom which crosses a navigable river ; and it will open to afford the largest vessels a free passage to and from the sea. Sir ED- WARD WATKIN, as the Chairman of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Rail- way Company, which has undertaken the work, is to be congratulated on the enterprise he has shown, and upon the determined way in which he has faced all difficulties. It is a , discredit to our Parliamentary system that al generation should have passed by since the first attempt was made to obtain permission to build this bridge across the Dee. But it has now been com- menced, and when it is finished the Railway Monopolists who have hitherto blocked the way will be subjected to that keen competi- tion which is good for Railway Companies in stimulating enterprise, and good for the com- munity in that it lessens the cost in the carriage of goods, and increases the facilities of the travelling public.

"Truth " says : " The surest way to a title is still to produce intoxlcating liquor of some sort. We have lately had several brewers converted into hereditary legislators, and I now see that the 'honour' of a baronetcy has been conferred upon a Dublin distiller. Let me plead for the retail bungs. Why are they to be left out in the cold ? It would be only fair to grant knighthoods to half a dozen publicans."

Tile Home Secretary does not believe in making fish of one and flesh of another in the matter of lotteries. In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, he said in reply to a question that he could not undertake to ex- empt persons from prosecution for lotteries for charitable purposes. It is satisfactory to see that there is less of lotteries at bazaars. Even the "unco guid" are beginning to say —"You must not do evil that good may come." The end does not always justify the means.

THE ways of "the great unpaid," like those of " the heathen Chinee," are peculiar; and it would seem just at present that magis- trates are disposed to conclude that most constables have something of the ENDACOTT about them. But it is very hard on a police- man who is doing his duty to be treated as though. to say the least of it, he had made a mistake. P.C. PARKER will undoubtedly think so when he reflects on the termination of the case in which he gave evidence at Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. Accor- ding to that evidence, he had seen a num- ber of men leave the Hermit Inn, Winwick, at eleven o'clock on the night of the sth inst ; and about five minutes afterwards he saw a man go to the back door with a jug in his hand. Presently he' came out of the house with beer in the jug, and was pro- ceeding to' follow the landlord's directions by going over the fence, when he was stopped by the constable. Challenged as to what excuse he could make for selling beer at that hour, the landlord replied that the beer had been filled before eleven o'clock, and was awaiting the customer. But this was not the line of defence taken in court by the land- lord's lawyer. He proceeded to cross- examine the constable as to the time, and asserted that Winwick Church clock was four minutes too fast. P.C. PARKER, however, stuck to his text, and affirmed that he had checked his watch by the Legh time signal. Will it be believed that, notwithstanding this, the Bench dismissed the summons on the ground that "the time was so near and close that they did not think it necessary for the case to be continued P" It comes to this as to the time, that the assertion of a paid ad- vocate, who was not on oath, and who was not present, 13 accepted in preference to that of a constable who was on oath, and who was present. It does not appear that the land- lord said anything about Winwick Church clock being too fast when he was "caught in the act "; but it does seem that he was con- scious of being in the wrong when he pleaded that the beer had been drawn before eleven o'clock. Further, it is pertinent to note that, according to the constable's evidence, the beer-hunter went to the back door. That might, of course, be that he was ashamed of being seeu going for beer, and preferred the back way—j.tst as he would if he was paying

Lord Stanley, of Alderley, has touched the Fair Trade pitch, and has become defiled. He wants to mend trade by ruining it with a duty of from ten to twenty per cent. on cer- tain imported articles. He does not perceive that things are made dearer by adding to their price. There is another Lord Stanley —he of Preston; and he once shrewdly said that when one gate was locked it was no relief to lock another. Lord Stanley, of Alderley, should ponder this saying, and grow wise.

Let bicyclists beware. A young man named Bent was summoned to the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for riding his bicycle on the footpath. He pleaded that the road was covered with stones, and, as the hearts of the magistrates were not as hard as the road, he was let off on paying the costs of the case. It may not always happen that the Bench will be so lenient, so let bicyclists beware.

The late Richard Jefferies had been long ill, and for some time his wife had to write for him to his dictation. The following ex- quisite passage formed a portion of the last article he wrote with his own hand They go on without me, orchis-flower and cow- slip. I cannot number them all. I hear, as it were, the patter of their feet—flower and buds and the beautiful clouds that go over, with the sweet rush of rain and burst of sun- glory among the leafy trees. They go on, and I am no more than the least of the empty shells that strewed the sward of the hill."

John Percival, of Earlestown, has got him- self in trouble by ordering and drinking a pint of ale at Lowton when he could not pay for it. He played his little trick on Sun- day, the 7th inst., by passing himself off as a bona fide traveller and bona fide customer. He would seem to be one of those who can say, in the words of the ancient rhyme : Back and side go bare, go bare, Both foot and hand go cold; But, belly, God send thee good ale enough, Whether it be new or old.

The forty pounds of dynamite said to have been found on a fashionably-dressed French- woman, at Cowes, turns out not to be dynamite at all. Col. Magendie finds that it is model- ling clay, and only three small cakes of that.

That little flourish about "Conspiracy to blow up Osborne House "was the outcome of the lively fancy of the reporter who was paid so much a line. Query : Will it be safe for the future to travel with cakes of any kind ? Better have them light-baked; if they are heavy, they may be "nabbed."

It was alleged that the defendant and another boy were in the field, and took away four turnips and left eight uprooted on the ground. The son of Kay gave chase, and captured Wiuterbottom, who was rescued from his grasp by several women. Harriett Platt, Elizateth Reughsedge, and Selina Keenagban, all of Warrington-road, were charged with assaulting George Kay. A large number of witnesses were called on each side, and in the end the Bench dismissed both cases. Mr. W. T. Hui- band was solicitor for the complainant, and Mr. J. W. Knowles for the defendants.

A Liverpool contemporary says :—" We learn that it is positively settled that the Queen will not visit Manchester this year. Her Majesty is said to be in need of rest, and is unable to undertake any more pub- lic duties during the present year." This means—if it means anything that the Queen will not cut the first sod of the Manchester Ship Canal, as has been ex- pected. But the statement comes from a source where the wish may be father to !he thought ; and it will be well, therefore, to await a more official, and, let us hope, a more favourable announcement.

The editor of the " Times " would seem to have not merely a slate, but the whole roof off when he refers to the leader of the Liberal party. Mr. Gladstone incidentally expressed himself on Tuesday as being in favour of the Channel Tunnel scheme, whereupon the " Times " suggests that he is endeavouring to purchase the support of the shareholders of the South• Eastern Railway! In the same speech Mr. Gladstone had a good word to say for milk. Does this mean that he was endeavouring to pur- chase the support of all the farmers and milk- men of the United Kingdom? Really, the Thunderer must be getting to the sixth age which " shifts into the lean ard slippered pantaloon."

UNJUST WEIonTs AT WI'DNES.—At Widnes Petty See' eon., on Thursday, Samuel Francis, greengrocer, Albert- road, was charged with using unjust weights.—On the 11th August a youth named William Prescet was hawking vegetables and fish through the town in a cart owned by the defendant. ALLEGED NEGLECT OF A CHILD AT WIDNES.—Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Tuesday morning held the adjourned inquiry at the Widnes Police Station into C's circumstances attending the death of the infant son of Michael Fox, chemical labourer, 37, Cromwell-street. The evidence given at the previous inquiry was read, and then Dr. Hutchinson deposed that he first saw the child on the 7th of March. At that time be was called in to see an elder child, and did not know that the deceased was suffering from any disease. On the 12th May he attended the child , for measles, and in June the mother called him in, and he found the child was suffering from debility. He prescribed for the child, but did not supply any medicine. He told Mrs. Pox to get it some chemical food, as it did not require any medicine. He was never called to see the child again. He did not remember telling the parents that the child would not recover, but he might have said that it was a delicate child. On Thursday last he made a post-mortem examination of the body. The child, which was nine months old, weighed 7lbe., which was about the average weight of a new born babe. The body was greatly emacia- ted, bat there were no marks of violence upon it. In the chest, stomach, and bowels here were alight traces of food. He found evidence of tuberculosis on both of the lungs and the abdomen. The cause of death was consumption of the bowels. This might be caused by an insufficiency of foed sr improper food, but there was no direct evidence to show that this was so in the present instance. In his opinion life would have been prolonged had the infant had proper medical and parental care.—Joseph Tracey, the relieving officer, deposed ,that Fox applied for the attendance of the parish doctor, hut as he was receiving 183 per week, and had three children, he (witness) told Fox he must make his own arrangement with a medical man. The child then ap- peared to be very poorly and delicate.—The Coroner asked the relieving officer if he did not think it would have been better to have granted the medical attendance asked for. He was not finding fault with the officer, for be be- lieved that the father ought to have paid, but if he was destitute at the time and could not pay it was very hard on the child —Witness replied that the majority of medical men in the town were willing to accept so mach per week from working men whose family had had attendance, and this man having a weekly wage he did not think he was entitled to free medical aid.—The mother, who was called, said she carried Gut the doctor's orders as to foed.—The jury brought in a verdict of death from " Natural causes," and added that they were of opinion that the parents had shown a certain amount of neglect in the care of their child —The Coroner, at the request of the jury, severely censured the parents, whose neglect he said was almost

THE WIDNES MAIN SEWERAGE SCHEME.—On Thursday Major Tullock, CE., an inspector to the Local CT' overnment Board, held an inquiry at the Public Offices into the Appli- cation ef the Widnes Local Board for sanction to borrow £lO,OOO for the purpose of extending the main sewerage scheme of the township. In addition to the members and officials of the Local Board the only ratepayers persent were , Mr. W. H. Kershaw and Mr. T. Sadler. Up to the present about £24,000 has been spent on main drains in the town- ship, and by the present system drains will be constructed in Victoria-road, Luasdale-read, Widnes-road, Albert road, Warrington-road, Moss Bank, and Ann-street. rhe drainage system of the town will then be almost complete —The sur- veyor (Mr. Higginson) produced maps of the district, and stated that ventilation would be provided by means of about nine brink chimneys. forty feet high, each of which would cost about £2OO and by 26 four inch cast and wrought iron tubes—ln reply to the inspec or, the surveyor said there wee no nuisances from the present sewers. There was no I system of ventilation in the streets,—Mr. Kershaw objected to the manner in which it was proposed t) dispose of Mill Brow sewage. He thought the drain ought to be laid in Albert-road instead of Moss Bank. He also obj-cted to the manner in which liic'oria-road sewer was being constructed. —The Inspector asked Mr. Kershaw if be had made any calculations as to the gradients, 4.tc, of the sewers be alluded j to.—Mr. Kershaw replied that he had not and the inquiry terminaied.—Tne Inspector afterwards inspected the dis- trict. He was accompanied by the clerk (Mr. J. T. Allen) and the Surveyor. MARRIA.OE OF LORD TOT.LEMACHE'S SON.—The marriage of the Hon. Douglas Tollemache, son of 1 Lord Tollemaclae, of Helmingham, with Alice Mary, eldest daughter of the late Mr. John Head, took I place on Wednesday afternoon in St. James's I Church, Piccadilly. The wedding party met at the ; church at a quarter to two. Mr. Arthur F. C. Tol-1 lemache acted as best man ; and the bridesmaids i were Miss Edith and Miss Muriel Head, the bride's sisters. The Rev. George F. Head, vicar of Christ Church, llampstead, and the Rev. Graham Keeling. of St. Andrew's, Brighton, uncles of the bride, were the officiating clergymen, the bride being given 1 away by her mother. The wedding party after- 1 wards reassembled at the house of Mr. Henry Head I (uncle of the bride), in Wimpole-street ; and later 1 in the afternoon the newly-wedded pair started for the Tyrol on their wedding tour. HARVEST QUEEN CORONATION AT LEIGH. On I Saturday afternoon the second annual event of crowning the Harvest Queen at Leigh was celebrated on a magnificent scale, and before a vast number of spectators. The processionists, numbering over 1,500, first met at Guest's Mill, and, having been I marshalled for procession, they filed out, and, ac- companied by the firs-lane and the St. Thomas's , Brass Bands, paraded the principal streets. The j various trades were represented. and in the proces- sion were the usual string of flower girls, Pole dan- cers, &o. The event was a great success, and it is I stated to be the finest of the kind ever held in the district. After the procession the party assembled in a field at Westleigh Lodge, where the ceremony. I of crowning the Queen, who is Miss Bessie Pilling,l aged fourteen years, daughter of Mr. J. Pilling, col- liery manager, was gone through in good style, fol- lowed by a number of hornpipe dances, plaiting of I , the ribbons, &c. ' . _

A SERVANT'S CLAIM.—At the County Court, QII Thursday afternoon, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, a case was commenced in which Kate Thompson, of Gooseberry Hollow, Norton, sued Wil- liam Whitlow, landlord of the ,Preston Brook Hotel, for the sum" of .£2 13s sd, the balance of wages alleged to be due to her as a domestic servant in the employ of the defendant. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Jenkins for the defendant. The claim was admitted, but Mr. Whitlow set up a counter claim for .£3 15s, which Mr. Jenkins con- tended was due because of the plaintiff leaving her situation to get maried, and so breaking her con- tract. His Honour disallowed .£1 lOs of the .f.. 3 15s counter-claimed; and evidence in support of the counter-claim was then given. From the evidence of Miss Whitlow, daughter of the defendant, it ap- peared that the plaintiff was engaged on a-yearly hiring in January last, and that on the 13th of May last she left the defendant's service without notice. This witness was under cross-examination when the court adjourned until next Thursday. POSTMEN AND THE NORTHWICH ELECTION.—In the House of Commons, on Thursday, Mr. W, Abra- ham asked the Postmaster-General whether, during the recent election for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, an agent of Lord H. Grosvenor employed a post office clerk at Runcorn to deliver circulars to the electors; if this clerk in turn employed other servants of the post office to deliver circulars, for which all were paid at the rate of one halfpenny each; if it was true that nearly 500 out of 3,000 cir- culars issued by the agent of the Liberal candidate were returned undelivered by the post office officials at Runcorn; if, when these circulars were submitted to the overseer, he pronounced most of the ad- dresses to be correct, and what action will he take with respect to the conduct of this official? Mr. Raikes said: The only officers of the post office at Runcorn who appear to have been concerned in the delivery of circulars during the recent election were five postmen who were employed for the purpose by a printer in the town, and did the work when off duty and without the knowledge of the postmaster. They state in explanation that they did not know they were doing wrong, being off duty, but I do not approve of the proceeding and have cautioned the men. 359 circulars issued by the Liberal candidate and 248 issued by the Conservative agent were re- turned undelivered on account of insufficient or in- correct address. lam assured that every possible effort was made to deliver them, many being sent out two or three times. On Monday afternoon the remains of John Dean, of Weston, were interred at Runcorn Cemetery. For a long time past Dean bad been a sufferer through ill health, and the best medical skill procered proved unavailing, and he died on Thursday, the 11th inst. Dean was a member of the first team of the Runcorn Football Club, and his clever sterling play amongst the forward division was fully recognised by the thousands of persons who have watched the matches. He was of a quiet unassuming disposition, ever ready to for- give and to torget an injury; and amid all the rough ex- citement of a foreball match he always maintained the same Rood-tempered demeanour. Ilia place will not be readily tilled, and his early demise was the cause of much sorrow amongst his fellow players. The funeral procession on Monday started from the house of the widowed mother of the deceased. The Rev; W. Bryant, curate-in-charge, and the officers of St John the Evangelist's Church, Weston, to which church the deceased during his lifetime be- longed, walked in front, and then followed the football players and other members of Runcorn Football Clot). Preceding the hearse marched the brass band of St. John's Sunday School, playing the Dead March in "Saul." The mourning coaches, containing the relatives and friends of the deceased. brought up the rear. The funeral service in the church and at the grave side was impressively conducted by the Rev. W Bryant. A largo number of wreaths were placed upon the coffin. One rent by the members of the Football Club w4e a fine specimen of artistic skill. I was composed of arum lilies, white stefran, white camilias, white geraniums, and roses; and was supplied by Mrs. Stoll, of High-street.

The report of the directors showed a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year of £87,756 lOs 2d, which, with £34,451 9s lid brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £122,208. The directors proposed to deal with the balance as follows: Dividend on preference capital at 'seven per cent. per annum, £10,850 18s 41; dividend on ordinary capital at twenty- five per cent, per annum, £67,812 lOs ; amount to be written off patents' account, £7,500; balance car- ried forward, £36,044 us 93,—0n the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. W. The fortnightly meeting was held *at Dutton —Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs J Lockwood, T Whitley, Mm.ers AITOD, Taylor, Htdfield, Hall, Brandreth, Thomas, Turner, 11 Lin. ker (clerk), and W H Linaker (deputy clerk).

THE RUNCORN SCHOOL FEES QUESTION. In the absence of Mr. Fisher, the Rev. J. I/tckwood moved that the school attendance officers to Runcorn School Board, Messrs. Thomas Bowyer and George Howard, be appointed school inquiry officers for the toe nehip of Runcorn at a salary of .£5 each for the respective districts. —Mr. S. Taylor seconded the motion.—ln reply to Mr. Brandreth, the Deputy Clerk explained that the salaries would be paid by the Runcorn tow ;ship, and not by the Union.—Mr. Brandreth said the Board were going to pay £lO for the purpose of bringing mwe people on the rates.— The Chairman replied that if the c tees were not deserving they would not be entertained.—Mr. Mclntyre would like to know who had done the work hitherto —Mr. Taylor asked whether Runcorn did not pay its propor- tion towards the salaries of the at lance °fa- cets in the Union. The Runcorn Schrol Beard paid its officers and he thought it was only fair that the Union should pay its'proportitto in thie Case.—Mr. Brandreth was of opinion that if the resolution was carried the duty of the officers would be to bring persons forward for the remission of fees, and thus add to the rates. Mr. Taylor said they were only asking for £lO a year to be paid to Messrs. Bowyer and Howard, whose duty it would be to report once a fortnight to the Guardians. If they did not enter into this arrangement they would perhaps have to pay about £BO a year ter the work. Mr. Branttreth : I hope not.—Mr. Taylor: We hope not, and we are trying to avoid that.—Mr. Hadfield added that the school fees would be paid by Runcorn.—Mr„ Brandreth again argued that it was in- tended to iscrease the cost of the work from £7 to £6O per annum, and be thought that an independent officer should be appointed Mr. Taylor said that if that was done they could not offer less than £6O or £7O a year, and then the work would not be done so efficiently as it would under the proposed system —The resolution was carried.

Mr. Aaron propo-,ed--Tbat the clerk commonicate with the following public bodies in the county of Cheshire: Cor- poration, Improvement Commissioners, Local Boards, Boards of Guardian., and Highway Boards, calling atten- tion to the self-elected representatives on the Weaver Trust, with a view to devising some scheme by which the Weaver will be managed by a body of trustees elected by the rate- payers of the county."—Mr. Taylor seconded the proposi- tion —Mr. Aaron asked how much the Weaver Trustees had paid to the county during last year,—The Clerk replied that the amount had been £5OOO in sotne years and less in others. TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT EARN WORTH. The members of the Farnworth Cburcb-of England Tem- perance Society held their annual demonstration on &tor- , day afternoon. The society, in its junior and senior sec- tions, has a membership of about 250, and 130 of these , assembled at the National Schools, and, headed by the beautiful banners of the society, they paraded through the village lanes. Music was supplied by the Widnes Jubilee Temperance Brass Band. On the route, the members made a stoppage at the residence of Mr. J rhn Brook, J.P., the hon. treasurer, and at the residence of Mrs. Iltbbert, who took a prominent part in the formation of tbe society seven years ago. The members then proce-ded to the church, where the Rev. J. Taylor Collins, curate of Walton on the Hill, preached an appropriate sermon. Subsrquently an ad- journment was made to a field, where various amusements were indulged in, but cold as+ d and an occasional fall of rain militated hard against the enjoyment of the party. A long programme of sports had been arranged. but owing to the weather could not be carried out. A 100 yards k race was won by P. J. McMahon, who received a gold bre pia, and a pocket knife was presented to Joseph wylde, came in second. Great interest was taken in a football match between R. Johnson's team, which included several widnes players, and the Fsrnworth Footbdi Club. The Widnes team won by one goal, one try, arid one minor, to Farnworth one minor. At a later period in the evening tear was provided and about 200 persons sat down at the tables, which were presided over by Mee. dames Bond, Baldwin, A. Carter, Beyword, Clarke,. Calland, and Wm. Davies, and the Misses Bond, Hilbert, Haddock, Fogg, A. Jameson, Hunter, Latchford, Jack, H. Glover, and Percival. Afterwards an entertainment was held under the presidency of Mr. Brock, and the room was crowded. The programme was sustained by the linyton Christy Minstrels, whose petformances gave the utmost satisfaction. On the motion ef the Rev JE. Lawton, se- conded by Mr. J. W. Davies, a coruial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Brock for presiding. Mr. Brock, in reply- ing, said be had for some time past made a careful observa- ' tion of crime in Widnes and in the country, arrt these ob- servations, so far as regarded Widnes, pointed distinctly to the fact that at least nine-tenths of all the ct,es tried in the Widnes Police Court could be traced directly or indirectly to drunkenness. He believed if there were no drunkardS thee, would have very little to do in the Widnes Police Court. but during the last two or three wears there had be-n a manifest improvement, which he put down entirely to the influence brought to bear on the populatien of the town by the various temperance societiee, and in these he included the Salvation Army. (Hear, bear.) Although they might not agree with that religious body's methods, still deserved their support and reel:wc,. (Hear, hear.) There they was no doubt that the Temperance Societies and the Salvation Army had had a distinct effect upon the morality of the town, and that should encourage them to persevere, and if every member of the Farnworth society would con- stitute himself a missionary for the cause, and try to bring his influence to beat upon some fellow workmen or frimds, their numbers would increase considerably, and OW WRAS tbe way to make the cause prosper. (Applause.)

SHOCKING REVOLVER ACCIDENT. -- On Thursday, at Wolverhampton, George Leonard Gananacß tawiaevn,l,3ly hot hi . son of Nmtr: Gannaway, taller, Darlington-street, c self with his father's revolver. The weapon, a six-cham- bered one, was on Thursday rnerning put by Mt. Dannaway under the shop counter, with one chamber charged. During the father's absence the boy got the firearm and presented it at the shop boy, Thomae Waldron. WAR:IZTON V. Orrotr.—Played at Warrington on Sat- urday, and the home team, winning the toss, put in the visitors. Montgomery and Sutton soon left, but Lorinur slowly raised the score to 40, when the latter was bowled. Of the ethers, Bigland, Power, and Court reached doable figures. Gregory played well, but be was decidedly lucky on several occasions, tie fielding on the home side net sus- taining the high character it has held for the past few few weeks. His innings included nine 4's, and a six— straight drive on the bowling green. The score reached 184. Tinsley was the most suocessful bowler. Warrington had not two hours' play, but nearly reached their opponents' total. Crosfield was out at five, and Tinsley at 32. Clarke joined Denton, and runs came at a great pace. Numerous changes were tried, but once being set, Clarke treated all alike, fours to the boundaries being the order of the score. The younger Gregory was knocked off by four boundaries in successive balls, and Gaskell gave way for 13 in an over. Clarke was out, after being in an boor, by a catch at short slip. He had compiled 67 by thoroughly sound cricket, hitting safely all round the wicket and without giving a chance. His score was made of fourteen 4's, a three, a two, and six singles. Denton played on soundly and steadily,and the score still rose. Woodhead was bowled for 22,and soon after time was called, with Denton 38 not out, and the score 162 for four wickets. Score:—

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The weather on Saturday was very unfavourable, and in consequence many matches in various pots of the country had to be abandoned. A lot of rain fell on Friday night and Saturday morning at Huddersfield, and there was no chance of resuming play, so the game between Fookehire and Middlesex was ultimately abandoned as a drawn one. At Birmingham there was less than an hour's cricket in the match between Warwickshire and Notts, which also had to be abandoned, Mr. Docker hit brilliantly, his 58 not out Including one 5 (four for an overthrow), ten 4's, a 3, and a 2. On the strength of his splendid performance in the match, it is said, Mr. Docker has been invited to join Shaw and Shrewsbury's team for Australia. The match between Surrey and Lancashire was resumed at the Oval on Saturday. Henderson and Mr. Ricketts ad- ded 26 runs for the seventh wicket, but the others did little, and the innings closed at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock a ith the total at 165, leaving Lancashire victorious by 147 runs. The annual Cheltenham cricket week commenced on Monday on the College ground, a game being begun be- tween Gloucestershire and Lancashire. Both counties were well represented, Lancashire having precisely the same team that so decisively beat Surrey last week, while for Glouces- tershire the only notable absentee was Mr. J. 11. Brain. The chief feature of the day was the superb batting of Mr.Ec- else, who went in when two wickets were down for ten runs, and stayed until the total reached 238, being eighth out for 113. He was in altogether three hours and a quarter. The longest stand of the day was made by Eccles and Briggs, when 84 runs were added. Briggs hit up 41 by ten 4's and a single. In the end the innings closed for 252. On Tuesday the hems county finished their innings for 132 and, following en, made 213 for eight wickets. Owing to adverse weather it was not until three o'clock on Wednes- day that Gloucestershire went on with their batting, and after the remaining wickets had added six to the total, Lan- cashire were put in to get exactly 100 to win. As the ground was playing queerly it seemed just possible that there would be a close finish after all, but the bold, free hitting of Scgga and Briggs and the steady batting of Bar- low soon settled matters, and by a quarter-past five the winning stroke was made, and Gloucestershire were beaten by six wickets. Arthur Shrewsbury, playing for Notts against Michlissex, on Tuesday, put in some remarkable batting. He remained at the wicket over ten boars, and scored 267. When he was eighth out the total stood at 536. Derbyshire, on Wednesday, at Kennington Oval, com- pleted their short but disastrous season of first-class matches. They were engaged six times,and were beaten on every occasion. Lancashire defeated them first by six wickets and then by 54 runs; Yorkshire beat them in one innings and 39 runs, and then in one innings and 163; while Surrey won against them in one innings with 237 runs to spare, and on Wednesday by 299 tans. In face of this it is difficult to see bow Derbyshire can henceforth be regarded as a first-class county. At a meeting of the Executive of the National Cyclists' Union, on Tuesday, it was agreed to find £5O to meet a similar amount voted by the C.T.C. for the purchase of a fresh supply of boards to be erected to warn cyclists of , dangerous parts of roads. This is a useful way of spending money, and will no doubt be the means of preventing some , accidents in the future. Mr. R. Todd, who has for some time held the important • po3t of secretary to the National Cyclists' Union adheres to his determination to resign his position. The reason given for this step is that he finds the work of secretary so heavy that bets unable to carry it on in conjunction with his own business.

Totals 10899 9118 719 In Marston there was a decrease in the poll of one in Weaverham of two, and in Wharton of five, so that the nett increase in the poll over the 1886 election is 711. There were 43 spoiled papers. Of the electorate according to the register, whioh is twelve months old, 84.8 per cent, were polled, and considering the large number of removals and deaths, this must be considered highly satistactory. It may be interesting to point out that in 1885 the figures I read thus: Brunner, 5,023; W. H. Verdin, 3,995; majority, I 1,028. In 1886 the figures were: R. Verdin, 4.418; Brunner, 3,958; majority, 458. Mr. Brunner therefore in the present contest polled 89 more votes than he did in 1885, and 1,154 more than he did in 1886, showing a most striking change. Lord Grosvenor, on the contrary, polled 12 less than the defeated Tory candidate in 1885, and 433 less thin the suc- cessful Unionist in 1886. There is not the slightest doubt that much is due to the increased energy shown by the Liberal leaders in the division, and the admirable work of the officials. Mr. W. Handle', the permanent secretary to the Divisen Association, deserves a special ward of praise. THE PktESS ON THEZELECTION. The "Freeman's Jouraal " says the Northwich electors have pronounced against the Government with an emphasis which cannot be mistaken, bat that doss not necessarily mean that the Government will he prevented from plunging into all sorts of adveetures in their Irish policy. Out of sheer desperation they may seek to do battle with the League, but they will find that to proclaim the League is one thing; to suppress it is something very different, The " Express, " the organ of the Orange and landlord party in Dahlia, speaks of the election as "a heavy blow to our confidence" and a "distinct success for the Gladsionien faction," but if a determined stand be made by the effective majority in Parliament "all may yet ba well." The" Irish Times" (Unionist) ascribes Mr. Brunner's victory to his personal claim,. The air was thickly charged. on Tuesday with "explana- tions" of the Tory-Unionist defeat at Northwich. The "St. James's Gazette" thinks that the Liberal Unionists voted for Mr. Brunner because the Government have not proclaimed the National League, and it urges Lord Salis- bury to prove to all the world that he is "in earnest and not afraid." If the Government are "going to be afraid of Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Parnell," says the" Gazette," " they might just as well not be where they are :" and it pro- mises them that if they will only follow up brave words by brave deeds "the voters who placed them in I power will rally to their support." Lord Salisbury will I probably derive little comfort from this advice. The " Times " remarks complacently that Mr. Brunner's victory r was" much more the victory of a candidate than of a cause," forgetting that Mr. Brunner is the same candidate I who was rejected last year. The " Times " urges Lord ' Salisbury to renew his efforts, and to "cope once and for ' all with the forces of disorder in Ireland." In other words, the Premier, who sees the country daily pronouncing r against coercion, is told that he will recover his popularity • if he throws off all restraint and uses to the full the powers conferred on the Government by the Coercion Act. The "Morning Post" courageously declares that Home Rule is in no more esteem in the Northwich division than it was a year ago; but still it regards the vote as a " minor defeat " of the Government, and remarks that it " may do r good service if it arouses Ministers to the necessity of • strengthening the Ministerial ranks, and of gaining thereby,

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THDDADAY.

Had the victory at Northwich stood by itself it would have been a startling event. But following as it does an almost unbroken series of Liberal vic- tories it is, as Mr. Gladstone says in his letter to Mr. Brunner, "an addition to evidence now some- what rapidly approaching to a demonstrative character" that the people of England have determined to do full justice to the people of Ireland. In the desperate depression of the earliest moments following the announce- ment of the figures, the "Times" made a miserable effort to pooh-pooh the result, and represented it as "much more the victory of a candidate than a cause." On further reflection, however, the hope- lessness of thus burying their heads in a sand heap has come home to the belated combatants, and the unmistakeable character of the result ts admitted. It would be impossible to cite in any previous epochs a parallel state of affairs. In the closing months of Lord Beaconsfield's Government, Tory succes- ses in the bye-elections in Southwark and Liverpool entrapped the Conservative party into a dissolution. But these were almost identical cases, where large borough populations were appealed to. In the bye- elections which have taken place this year, and which have with one exception either wrested a seat from the Conservatives or materially reduced their majority, we have every class of the national body of electors represented. In Nortlrwich,Spald- ing, and Basingstoke, we have composite constitu- encies where the agricultural and the town vote are , mixed. In, North Paddington and Brixton, where the Conservative majority was reduced fifty per cent, we have ~two sections of the metropolitan con- stituency. In Burnley and Coventry, where seats were won from the Mimsterialists, and in Glasgow where the Liberal majority was nearly doubled, we have the borough vote pure and simple. Thus it is not Liberalism triumphant in boroughs and defeated in counties, nor is it that the agricultural vote is neutralised by that of the working man in town. The series of Liberal advances, culminating in the crowning victory of Northwich, show that in all classes of votes and in all types of constituency the tide has turned, and is now flowing fast In favour of the Liberal party. The effect of the Northwich election upon both political parties is striking. The Ministerialists are plunged in the depths of apathetic despair' whilst Liberals are full of hope and confidence for the future. The next fight will be in Huntingdonshire, and though it is regarded in the Liberal camp as too much to hope to carry this Tory stronghold, it is determined to make a stout fight, and it is ex- pected that the Conservative majority will be materially reduced. Meanwhile everyone is agreed .that the Government cannot any longer carry on as it is at present constructed. There are pitiful cries for Lord Hartington to go to its assistance, and confident statements are put forth pointing to a re- construction of the ministry which is to-take place in November, and will amount practically to ex- tinction of Tory supremacy, with a compositeparty, which, after all, is much more largely composed of Conservatives than of Dissentient Liberals. In As- suming the speculation to be true, I think that cer- tain important considerations are entirely lost sight of, The Conservatives may, truly, desire to have the assistance of Lord Hartington in their councils, but what they want still more is votes, and -what is the use of surrendering a considerable proportion of the loaves and fishes to Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamber- lain, and Sir Henry James if they cannot bring over with them an appreciable contribution of support among the electors? The Government is of course safe as long as the present Parliament exists. But that cannot be long in face of the state of public feeling disclosed by recent elections. There must be a General Election, when, unless matters mightily change, the Dissen- tient Liberals will be absolutely extinguished. On the other hand, what are Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain to gain by allying themselves with a doomed party? They have gone a long way to- wards making their severance from the Liberal party complete and irrevocable. But they have not yet burned their boats. It is not safe to ,predict what man may do in moments of desperation. But I think it will be well, for the present at least, to receive with caution these confident and circum- stantial assertions of pending coalitions. If any step in that direction is made, it will, I fancy, be confined to Lord Hartington.s finally drifting into the Tory harbour. Mr. Chamberlain, even when he most plainly loses his temper, is too astute a man thus to commit political suicide. The public occasionally hears something of the gentleman who signs himself W. Leathern Bright, and is commonly known in the House of Commons as " Willie " Bright. But the eldest son of the once great Liberal Tribune (Mr. J. A. Bright) has hitherto kept apart from politics. He has now, perhaps involuntarily, made himself known, and in not very happyrOircumstances. Be has, it appears, been attempting to rally the Dissentient Liberals in Rochdale, and is bound to admit that though he has piped they will not dance, though he has called they will not come. Mr. J. A. Bright insists that there are such phenomenon as Dissentient Liberals in Rochdale, besides his father and himself, but frankly admits that as they won't reply he is "dis- couraged from taking any further steps in the mat- ter," whatever the matter may have been; this adhesion of his eldest son to the new kind of Toryism called Unionism must compensate Mr. Bright for the falling away of his younger son, the member for Stoke. In spite of the alternative of incurring his father's resentment, which I believe is pretty openly expressed, " Willie " Bright has stood steadfastly by the Liberal flag, and has by his vote frequently counterbalanced that of his father, given in these latter days against those generous Liberal principles of which lie was once not the least illus- trious and successful exponent. In the "World" this week is an article on "Relics," meaning men who not only survive their contemporaries, but are in some sort representatives of their systems, their ways, and their thoughts. Going through the various professions, it is re- marked as perhaps worth notice." that the House

So far, so good—presumably the knees ; and those who remember it declare that it was an instructive and edifying sight to see a fat gentleman, vote is worth the trouble of fetching, though it with bare legs below his short overcoat, waddling won't "fetch" so much in coin of the realm as in through the snow up Brooklyn Heights to his house at the so-called good old times when it was a market- two o'clock in the morning, able commodity. A burly Irishman, with Home Rule looming be- fore him in the vista of the future, and with bitter- ness at his heart as he thinks of how he was be- guiled not long a4o into voting for an enemy of his dear " Ould Oirelattd," next tramps awkwardly up to answer an objection to his name remaining on the list. The oath is administered and Pat prepares for punishment at the hands of his questioner, the representative of the party making the objection. "Have you been in prison during the last twelve or eighteen months?' "No son.' "Recollect you are on oath !'' " Yez, non, oi know that same." "-Have you during that time been brought before the magistrates?' The weak place in his armour is found, and the shaft strikes home. " Yez, sorr ; an menny's the toime." He has, he admits, been fined within the last twelve months, but his " marster shelled out" and saved him from prison. Pat does not see why his failings, the principal one of which is probably a liking for the ale out of which the member for Warrington has secured so many of the good things of this world, should lose him his vote, and neither does the Barrister, who over-rules the objection, vastly to the delight of the son of Erin. Poor' Path He does not like remind- ing of his misdeeds. He had heard of how a cer- tain brewer made much money by investing in ale, and straightway proceeded to invest his one humble talent in the same enterprise, but it has worked badly for him. True, they both alike in- vested-their money in beer, but in one case it in- creased a hundred-fold, and in the other it passed cver the counter never to return whence it came. The same investment, but with a difference—what a mighty difference! And what a sad difference for so many! But to business again. A young man puts in appearance. He is a lodger, and, having answered a number of questions as to the terms on which he rents his rooms, &c., to the satisfaction of the Bar- rister, he also gets the vote. Then another lodger , claimant who does not answer the questions in the I same satisfactory manner is refused, and so on. So the round goes on. Now a householder's claim, now an objection, and now a lodger claim. Occasionally there are incidents, and legal argu- ments too, but one gets weary of the sameness. It is prosaic. Especially so are the arguments, and to a man whose only aim in life does not happen to be to kill time, an hour or two in a Revision Court should suffice. To claim a vote is not, if you have anything of a case, at all a formidable matter. Of course, if a person goes with the intention of trying to obtain a vote to which he is not entitled, and is not alto- gether as particular as he should be in avoiding the besetting sin attributed to Ananias, he runs a chance of getting himself into trouble, but in that case he has only himself to blame. Again, anyone who does not care to go to the Court unassisted, has only, to lay his case before the representative of his particular party, and he will find most of the trouble taken off his hands. When manhood suffrage takes the place of the present hemmed-in 1 and barricaded franchise, this ponderous official 'machinery will take a back seat. The sooner that 1 time comes, the better it will be.
AN EARLVSTOWN CONTRACTOR CHARGED WITH DRUNKENNESS.

Before Messrs. H. Houghton and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Joseph Pennington, contractor, Earlestown, and residing at Winwick, was summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly on the 3rd inst. Defendant pleaded not guilty, and was represented by Mr. Knowles.—P.C. Parker deposed that about quarter-past ten on the night of the date named he saw the defendant in charge of a horse and trap passing along the road in the direction of his own home. He was sitting, or half reclining, on the seat, and witness took charge of the trap about 500 yards from his own home; and on getting into the lane leading to defendant's house defendant's wife said the defendant came home that way every day, and if he (the constable) did not report her husband she would report him for not doing his duty. The defendant began to push witness about and challenged him to fight.— Mr. Knowles said he was instructed very differently to the evidence of the officer. He was told that the defendant was quite sober, and he would call evi- dence in support of that statement. He remarked that according to the officer's statement it seemed a pity that defendant's wife should try to have her husband prosecuted. He (Mr. Knowles) did not want to say anything about domestic differences in that court, and that matter had nothing to do with t the case. —The defendant. Joseph Pennington, was then sworn. He said he was returning home after doing some business at Earlestown, on the night in question. He met Mr. Howbridge at the Vulcan and had some conversation with him on business mat- ters. lie was perfectly sober, and the constable did not lead his (defendant's) trap, and he nevq stopped it. He nodded to the policeman on the way home. Ile was quite steady when he got out of the trap, and he never saw or heard his wife having any con- versation with the officer. In reply to Superinten- dent Weir, defendant said he had some drink during the day but he was quite sober. He would swear he never saw or heard his wife complaining to' the constable. He did not challenge the officer to fight, but he ordered him off his premises. Mr. John liowbridge, foreman at the works of Messrs. Vicars, Earlestown, said he met the defendant after nine o'clock on the night in question. Defendant was then quite sober, and they talked about an intricate matter of business calculation. The defendant was perfectly rational and sensible. In reply to Super- intendent Weir, witness said there was not the least appearance of drink upon the defendant. Patrick Finegan, an Irish labourer, deposed that he was at Mr. I'ennington's house when the defendant came home. Defendant was quite sober and steady. The defendant's wife did not speak or complain to the constable.—The Bench dismissed the case.

A tragic death occurred In Birmingham on Tuesday. Detective sergetnt Dobbs went into a house in seatch of a man. The wife opened the door, and was so startled at the officer's appearance that sbe fell back in a fainting fit and died immediately. At Greenwich Police Court on Tuesday, Rachel Talbot, of the San-in-the-samds public house, was fined £5O for adulterating beer with water. Excise officers found a beer engine employed which introduced water into the barrel ae the beer was drawn off. - -

Xetters to the editor. THE WARRINGTON GASWORKS. Sir,—When Mr. Alderman Holmes, as Deputy Mayor, was in the chair at the meeting of the Town Council held in July last, he stated, in answer to a question put by Mr. Councillor B ton as to when the accounts of the Corpora- tion would be discussed, that the accounts could only be discussed when the estimates are made. But the Gas Com- mittee never give estimates, so their accounts are not dis- cussed at all. I would ask, has the work done by the Gas Committee been satisfactory? Has not the time arrived when something more should be done than what has been done? As the present committee will not give any infor- mation respecting the works should not a Public Meeting be held, say, in the Working-men's Club, to see what steps can be taken?.—Yours truly,
Warrington, August 19th, 1887.

WHAT ABOUT NORTHWICII? Sir,—The thing is settled; Hartington, Chamberlain: Bright and Co. might as sell throw up the sponge at once. The people, after a short lapse, are MICR more pulling them- selves together for another mighty effort. Great political questions, like all epoch-making movements, can only make themselves accepted by the people after due and reasonable time for consideration. It is no use, Mr. Editor, the Eviglish people are a conservative race; they bold tenaciously to all tbe old superstitions handed down to them from their forefathers. Year after year, we see the feeble grala relaxing, and ail the old land-marks passed by, one hy one. Now it is the fetish worship of dukes that is going, family kfluence ; and all that in the good old days gave prestige to a ',aided aristocracy is threatened with the judgment of King Demos. 'I he answer given last Saturday at Northwich to the siupid letter of John Bright concern- ing Dr. Ingram's book should satisfy him and his colleagues that a little more discretion in letter writing would be ad- visable. If John had in years past studied the Irish ques- tion more freely he would have saved himself from the con- tempt which is sure to follow his letter of August S:h. The G.O.M. has proved in every question he has taken in hand that his and every man's duty is to make himself first ac- quainted with all the facts, histori.lal and otherwise.— Yours, ctn.,
SALT PANS.

LANE? Sir,—About twelve months ago you were favoured with an account of the in and outdoor licensed houses in and around our neighbourhood, which number about tan within a radius of 350 yards from the proposed site of

another. We have a full off spirit licensed house within 15 yards on one side and another within 35 yards on the other s;de of the proposel site, an,l yet this number, it appaars, is deemed by some interested persons of not sufficient accom- modation for the rtquirements of the neighbourhood, but must needs attempt to thrust a third noon us. How mind- ful some are of the future comfort and welfare of others.' We seldom hear of anyone applying for any of our medical men to come and reside in certain neighbourhoods to be ready in case of sudden attacks of sickness. I submit, sir, that if it were necessary to have more privileges in this business in this part of the town, it would be preferable to give it to one of the already existing houses that lie close to the proposrd site, than to add another to the already long list. I cannot but th'nk that the licensing magistrates and our temperance friends will do well to take note of this matter for the benefit of the neighbourhood.—l beg to remain. yours sincerely,
A RESIDENT.

THE TEMPERANCE CAUSE. Sir,—Poor" Uncle Toby " eeems to have quite lost his temper. What with his " Cockers " and " Colensos," his' sham philanthropists," his "humptuous and immodest" people, his delicate allusion to " sheer impertinence," Soc., he has altogether a very choice vocabulary of epithets. After such a display, it is perhaps as well that Uncle Toby should have the modesty to suppress his name. The cause of alcohol will scarcely gain by the advocacy of abuse. I might well decline to reason with such a man. I shall certainly riot bendy Billingsgate with him. But with TOW permission I will explain to Uncle Toby " what he is pleased to call my •` p tradox," namely. that brewers do most trade in the haunts of poverty. Ido not think it requires a " Colenso " to explain this, nor much intellect to grasp it. While the rich man is sipping his wine, the poor man drinks beer, and too often spends a very large proportion of his in- come in this beverage. I do not think I should be beyond the mark were Ito say that for every pint of beer taken by the rich, a quart is consumed by the poor. Learn, then, my "Uncle Toby," and strive to grasp this most" abstruse" of facts, that the brewer gets most money from him who con- sumes most of his liquor. I mean the poor man. I shall not write again on this subject. I should not have trespassed on your space at all had it not been for an attack made upon a meeting of the Warrington Temperance Federation, which, as secretary. I felt bound to notice. Thanking you, Mr. Editor, for your courtesy, I beg to remain, yours faithfully,

He is against the whole movement, thinking the workiug-man, wherever he may live, or whatever his occupation, should tramp to Bold-street whenever he wants to do an hour's reading. I have said nothing as to what the two big brewers might do ts counteract their evil work in the town. If Inv friends of the Temperance Federation will bear with my inconsis- tency, I would suggest that the brewers and the publicans show their magnanimity by raising a fund and placing it in the Mayor's hand° for the purpose of freeing the library. If they don't do this. I can only come to the condo. sion that they think they have done their ditty in sending us their juice and leaving us to stew in it. Again allow me to repeat that the two committees should be called together, and steps taken to make a November issue of the library question.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. IFROM OUR OWN CORRIZSPONDENT. 23, Old Broad-street, B.C. The Stock markets have been inactive during the week, but in spite of this oppressive dulness prices are being maintained. The most noticeable feature has been the fiactnations in Mexicans. and during the past few days we have been afforded a striking illustration of how the mar- ket is rigged, and bow impotent the most carefully formed judgments become in the face of an organised opposition. There is on the staff of a well known journal a gentleman who has attained a world wide celebrity as a finaecial authority. His predictions during the past twelve months have been simply marvellous in their accuracy. His means of information have been unique, and he has not only made a small fortune himself by acting upon his tips, but he has allowed the public to 'stand In " with praiseworthy disin- teres,edness. Among other securities on which he is an authority, judging by the result' of his advice, is Mexi- cans. Three weeks ago, when they stood at 61. or 62, he advised buying for a rise. Regarded from the point of view lof reason and carnation sense. Mexicans ought •o have gone up by leaps and bounds. The country was prosperous and increasing in prosperity, the construction of new railways released thousands of tons of produce in store, railway traffic returns showed a big increase, and there was not lacking a single necessary sign of improvement. Yet, oddly enough, Mexican stock began to decline. In spite of favourable re- ports of all kinds, it fell rapidly, and at the last settlement it stood at 941 as against 62 when the writer mentioned ad- vised buying for the rise. The secret was that a combined bear raid was being made upon the stock for the purpose of cornering the profit. There was less than half-a-dozen brokers in the ring, but they were influential, and the crowd , always "follow the money." on the Stock Exchange as on the turf. The fact that such authorities as Jones, Brown, and Robinson were selling Mexicans was accepted by the mob as sufficient justification for a general sell out. Every. body sold Mexicans, and the result nas been a huge crash. The unfortunate object of the attack had to realise at a big loss, said to amount to £30,030, though it is hoped and be- lieved to be mach less than this figure, while the bears have scored tremendously. Now mark the sequel. Directly the profit completed to realise at a loss, the reaction set in, and on Wednesday Mexicans were at one time better. The financial opponents of the Channel Tunnel scheme , are not lessened by the addition of Mr. Gladstone to its ' supporter& Financial circles are unanimous in condemning the undertaking, believing it to be financially unsound,l apart from the ever-present invasion scare which would be dragged out on the least provocatioe, and check legitimate business. It becomes a question quite apart from political whether it is wise to add to the list even if a tew specula- I tors would be benefited thereby. Granting the financia success, what is there to prevent a second company, whichl by the way, has been in existence for some time? A meeting of shareholders of Hutchins and Crowslev, Limited, London, was held on Wednesday at St. John's Wood, at five o'clock in the evening. This company has , been so severely criticised, both by the shareholders and the press, that the directors took care to avoid a repetition of such an objectionable mode of treatment, and therefore re. fused admission by holding it at such a time and place.' This is all the more striking,because a large majority of the shareholders reside in the country, and singularly enough , over 10,000 shares are held in Warrington. however, the directors have defeated their object by attracting notice, which they would not otherwise have done, in the course. they have adopted.

WARRINGTON INTERCEPTING DEPOT. Sir,—Yeur correspondent, "S. M.." in last Saturday's " Examiner," in meddling with these depots and mildly try- ing to colour them up, little knows upon what dangerous , ground he is treading, and be being an interested person, or 1 the tool of interested persons, one would have thought that as far as be was concerned he would have allowed the matter 1 to drop—l mean until the chairman, Mr. Alderman Burgess, ; had made his statement. This question Is too serious, and we want none of his bolstering. Drought or no drought will not dispense with the sickening odours from these places. Your correspondent save we must wait, the scheme , is not complete, and we have lemons to learn. Surely a I long time ago, with trumpet sound, a number of gentlemen were invited to witness its completion, and therefore we have a right to ask what is there to be done yet? Has it not coat enough? I repeat again the scheme has not 001314 up to the expectations of its originators, and that it will ultimately prove a failure. The Chairman of the Sanitary Committee has now been absent from the last two Council meetings, whether evading the explanation which Mr. Councillor Platt requires or not I cannot say. It is the desire to hesr the chairman'n defence of these depots that keeps my pen still to some extent. At present I will only hope that a coroner's inquest will not have to point out the •m; danger of the Howley depol; before myself, for part of a building, with a dangerous ditch along one side of it, with all the washings from the depOt running into it, and requir- ing to be held tip with about 50 props, reflects little credit on either architect or krilder.—Yours truly, WILLIAM DIGGLE. 5:4"- Wellington-street August 19tL, 1887.

IS 1T LEGAL? Sir,—A correspondent in your last issue very pertinently puts a phase to the front respecting the Free Library ques- tion, that has not been sufficiently pressed. Yin.: that of forcing the townspeople to subscribe for the loan of books which they have already bought and paid for. I wish to ask, sir, would it not be worth while to take opinion upon this question ? If it is legal to charge a penny rate for a given purpose, is it also legal to charge for the same par- pose in another fashion? I understand there are two committees that have had the work so far, in hand. Is it not possible to join the two forces, and by this means bring the movement to a success- ful issue ? There is no doubt of one thing, we cannot, we must not, I let the thing drop. The Town Council, in the high-handed I way they dealt with Mr. Monks' letter and Mr. Morris' offer, have not given any proef of a real desire to set the Library free. They have confessed to its being a question of ways and means. If this be all that is in the road, they are not worth supporting five minutes longer if they don't remove it. If no further attempt is made, let us marshal our forces for next November and see who is master. There seems to be a dearth of public spirited men in Warrington. Surely the town has some claim on its sons, or is it all the other way about? One may travel from Warrington Bridge to Longford Bridge, from Sankey Bridge to the Cemetery, and not find one resident holding the position of employer at any of our large works Ho ugh ton's, Rylands, Dal lam Forge, Bewsey, Cockhedge, Chemical Works, all the employers living far away from "the madding crowd." Having spoiled the Egyptians they are aaietly living upon the spoil. I ask Is it policy for them to do this thing? With their private libraries and their billiard room, bow smoothly life glides along. Recreative and intellectual pleasures within call, these people selfishly ignore us who are creating their wealth. I venture to say that it would be hard to find another town in England so utterly consigned to all that is cheap and nasty as is Warrington, by those whose duty it is to see that the schoolmaster shall have every help And encouragement In the work he has to do. The Jubilee Year has come ; it will pass away, and what shall we have in remembrance of it? As I prophesied early in the year, if the poor ctred to do anything well and good, the r:ch only would subscribe to make firmer the props that support the system whereby they eat, drink, and are merry. It seems almost to have been a principle in the past fora Warringtonian to watch and encourage other towns in their efforts to provide educational means for their sons. m i Mr. Bea ont, n a letter to the Mayor, dated September ! 20, 1883, could but . praise Manchester and Liverpool for their efforts in establishin.e, schools and classes for teaching law and medicine. Warrington being equi-distant of the two towns, her sons could pay their railway fare and reap the same benefits. Four years ago, he evidently thought Warrington only a baby, for he says—" Animals that are the longest lived take the longest time to attain their full age, and our great river which was a rivulet at its rise, bears a navy on its stream before it reaches thesea.." I wonder if Mr!!. Beamont thinks the town has attained its full age, Or is full grown. lam afraid not; otherwise he would not be so determined to keep it in leading strings. In a letter to the Library Committee, dated October sth, 1882, the Chair- man of our Library Committee (Mr. Beamont) reports at- tending a meeting of the Library Associatian at Liverpool, Sir J. Pluto in the chair. The chairman advised " that every effort should be made to make libraries as extensively useful as possEle to all classes to encourage the reading of biography, travels, and history." Mr. Beamont wrote that he was pleased to report this. May I ask him has he car- ried out his promise that he would Use all his influence to Effect this? Is he not rather the one stumbling block in the way ? I assert that it is an open secret in the town, among
