MR. J. T. BRUNNER. MP. The career of Mr. John Tomlinson Brunner, who has achieved such a notable victory for Home Rule in the Northwich Division, has been in some respects a remarkable one. Though of English birth, he is of German-Swiss extraction, and it may perhaps be inferred that his strong and consistent advocacy of self-government for Ireland is in no little due to his intimacy with the history and people of the Swiss Republic, for in that State the system of Federal Home Rule is followed with the happiest results. Mr. Brunner's father, who was a native of Zurich, settled in England and established a school in Liverpool. Mr. Brunner was born in 1842, and received a commercial education at his father's school. Having completed his school life in 1857. he entered upon a mercantile career. For a number of years he occupied a position in the office of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., chemical manufacturers,' Widnes, at which place Mr. Ludwig Mond was also employed -as a chemist. In 1872 he entered into partrership with Mr. Ludwig Mond, the eminent chemist, and together they were instrumental in starting the alkali works at Win- nington, near Northwich. The remarkable success which has attended this enterprise is well' known, and is due alike to the great business capacities of Mr. Brunner, and the aelentific genius of his emi- nent colleague. These works, it is said, are now the largest of their kind in the world, and they have been the means of employment of a great number of people, and have also materially added to the prosperity of the district in which they are situated. One of Mr. Brunner's main characteristics is a generous zeal for the advancement of education, and his benefactions and good works in this direction are numberless. His' gift of a free public library, at a cost of about .27,000, has well earned him • the distinc- tion of being the "greatest benefactor Northwich ever had." The library, which is a model of its kind, was opened in July, 1885, amidst a scene of public rejoicing, by the Duke of Westminster, the father of Mr. Brunner's latest opponent at the poll. The formal conveyance of the property stated" That the fee simple of the whole of the free library, and ' the ground upon which it stands, the ground in the rear, and the ground upon which the shops stand, shall be handed over to the Local Board of North- wich for the purpose of a free public library." In addition to this munificent- gift, Mr. Brunner has further advanced the cause of education in North- wich by founding Brunner scholarships in connec- ' tion with the Grammar School of which he is a trustee. Liverpool University College and Pam- worth and Witton Grammar Schools have also been herkefited by Mr. Brunner's generosity. Twelve months ago, when the Widnes Free, Library was formed, Mr. Brunner presented .£lOO towards the scheme, and the committee expended the money in the purchase of a number of scientific works which have the distinctive title of "The Brunner Collec- tion." Ile has recently given .£2OO towards Nant- wich Free Library, and has contributed a sum of money sufficient to obtain a site for the Winsford Free Public Library. In politics Mr. Brunner al- ways took a keen interest, and he was one of the I most generous and consistent supporters of the de- funct Mid-Cheshire Liberal Association. He was for several years hon. treas. of the Association. Mr. Brun- ner was first elected to Parliament in 1885, when, as the selected representative of the Liberal party of the Northwich Division. he defeated, at the general election of that year, Mr. W. H. Verdin, the Conservative candidate, by a majority of 1,028. He was assiduous in his attendance on his Parlia- mentary duties till the dissolution of 1886 on the Home Rule issue, when he was opposed by Mr. R. Verdin (brother of Mr. W. H. Verdin), who stood as a Liberal Unionist. The result of a contest which was fought with spirit and determination on both sides was that Mr. Brunner was placed in a mino- rity of 458. The memorable contest which has just closed, and which has ended in Mr. Brunner's re- turn to the House of Commons by more than his original majority, was, it will be remembered, caused by the death of Mr. H. Verdin. Mr. Brun- ner, it may be mentioned, has been twice married. His first wife was Salome, daughter of Mr. James Davies, of Liverpool, and his second, Jane, daughter of the late Dr. Wyman, of Kettering, Northampton- shire. Mr. Brunner is a county magistrate for Cheshire, and for many years has taken an active part as a member of the Northwich Board of: Guar- ilians. His residence is Winnington Old Hall, near Northwich.

RECEPTION IN THE HOUSE. On Tuesday, Mr. Brunner took his seat in the House of Comnions, and, as was to be expected, he met with a very hearty welcome from the members on the Liberal side of the House. Describing the scene the "Manchester Guardian" says :—" By the time Mr. Smith had been permitted to refuge to his seat on the Treasury bench. all the Opposition benches both above and below the gangway, although not overcrowded, were thoroughly well filled—possibly for the last time this session—in ' honour of Mr. Brunner. Far in the rear Mr. T. W. Russell could be descried, but no other Liberal Unionist was visible, and Mr. Shaw Lefevre was free to occupy the end of the front bench, along- side Mr. Childers, Mr. Bryce, Mr. Mundella, Mr. Fowler, and Mr. Broadhurst. In due course Mr. Brunner came down to the bar, where he stood with Mr. John O'Connor, both being festively arrayed in snowy vests, while Mr. Brunner had the return to I the writ in his breast pocket, where it presented the appearance of a floral decoration. Mr. Ar- nold Morley having joined them, the trio advanced up the floor amidst thundering cheers from Parnellites, Radicals, and Liberals, one broad smile a satisfaction spreading over the entire Op- position as the hero of the hour calmly went I through the ceremony of induction. SomebOdy below the gangway called for • Three cheers for I Northwich r as the hon. gentleman passed along in I front of the row of disconsolate Ministers; and when, having completed an unusually long conver- sation with the Speaker, he walked off behind the Ichair towards the Opposition benches, a sarcastic exclamation uttered in a stage whisper of Another blessing in disguise' increased the misery cof the mute Ministerialists." The " Liverpool Mercury" refers to the event as follows :—" The Liberal Unidikists did not put in an appearance this afternoon at the time when Mr. Brunner took his seat for Northwich. They are not much given to being present when any candidate at a bye-election is led up the floor of the House, and evidently find it much more comforting to their feelings to remain away. Mr. Brunner was marched up the floor to- day 'between Mr. Arnold Morley, the Liberal Whip, and Mr. John O'Connor, an Irish Home Ruler. The selection of'Mr. O'Connor was a tribute not only to the principles which Mr. Brunner represented, but also to the aid which he had received during his contest from Home Rule members. His reception was an ovation. When the first burst of cheering died down, an enthusiastic Irishman yelled out, Three cheers for Northwich,' and after he had signed the roll of Parliament and shaken hands with the Speaker, another irrepressible Irishman shouted out, 'Another blessing in disguise.' These ejaculations were received, of course, with laugh- ter; and Mr. Brunner having taken his place on the Liberal benches, the House went at once into com- mittee on the Coal Mines Regulation Bill." LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE. Mr Brunner has been the recipient of the follow- ing letter of congratulation from Mr Gladstone,
viz.:-
" Ilawarden, Chester, August 16, 1887. "Dear sir,—' congratulate you cordially on your triumphant return for the Northwich Division. , I

do not doubt that your personal character and posi- ' tion have much contributed tô. the result, but your opponent was also very highly favoured in name and associations, and few will seek to disguise the unquestionable addition thus made to the evidence, • now somewhatrapidly approaching to a demonstra- tive character, that the people of England intend to do full justice to the people of Ireland by confiding to them, in a spirit alike generous and wise, the Management of their own properly Irish affairs. I cannot but feel a particular pleasure in the large- ness of your majority. It is, indeed, to be lamented that years of the precious legislative life of a coun- try should be spent upon a controversy which can only end one way. Still, while it is important that the judgment of the nation should be speedy, it is yet more important that when it comes it should be unequivocal and decisive.---/ remain, faithfully yours,
4' W. E. 13Tak.nsToNE:'
MR. BRUNNER'S REPLY..

• Mr. Brunner[M.P., has addressed the following communication to Mr. Gladstone, in reply to his letter of the previous day:— House of Commons, Atig. 17, 1887. • Dear Mr. Gladstone,—l am very grateful to you for your letter. It will be a great help at the next contest. The "Times" speaks of my effrontery in describing the victory in the Northwieh Division as that of the masses over the classes. It was a sadly true statement. I know the constituency thoroughly, and can assure you that to the best of my know- ledge out of 5,112 votes in mv favour less than the odd 12 came from houses In the division of the annual value of ..£4O. There are, of course, many Liberal farmers who pay a larger rent, including land. The enthusiasm and devotion of the working men gave the greatest delight. One working man walked from Leek, in Staffordshire; one came from Newport (Mon.) ; one from Mostyn; one from Abergele ; another from Coventry; another from Fleetwood ; and two from Middlesbrough—all. of course, at their own expense. It will interest you to know that after (1) the sympathy with your generous proposal to confer upon the Irish people the management of purely Irish affairs, and to en- trust to them the responsibility for the mainten- ance of good order in Ireland, and after (2) the in- dignation excited by the Coercion Act, the feeling which most strongly influenced the electors in my favour was their hearty accord with my declara- tion in favour of the system—one man, one vote. Please accept my grateful thanks, and believe me, yours most faithfully, Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone.
• Join.; T. BRUNNER.

In addition to the instances of sacrifice made by working men at the recent election may be men- tioned the case of a Runcorn working man who was spending his holidays in Suffolk. Although his visit had not expired by i five days, he spent all Fri- day in returning home n order to be able to vote for "Justice to Ireland" on the following day.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

From one of the Beacons at Dartmoor, the eclipse of the sum was seen for nearly three minutes soon after sunrise, on Friday. The Rev. Dr. Parker, minister of the City Temple, left London for Liverpool, en route to America, on Friday afternoon. The artillery camp at Shoeburyness broke up on Friday in good order. The discipline maintained has been excel- lent, and no one remains in hospital. A communication was on Thursday night despatched to the Governor of Winchester Gaol from the Home Secret iry finally respiting the execution of the convict Augustus Early. The first meeting of the creditors of Mr William Cope. land Borlase, ex-M.P. for the St. Austell Division of Corn- wall, was held in London, on Friday. The liabilities were stated to be £43 653. SERIOUS RIOT IN IRELAND.—A serious r:ot occurred at Kenmore on Friday morning. The police used.their swords in charging the people, and several were injured. The police b trracks was stoned. Several arrests were made. THE LIPSEI Drsccosonas.—The friends of Lipski re- ceived information from Birmingham, on Friday, which is ex.Jected to lead to the identification of the man who pur- chased the nitric acid at Buchner's shop in Houndsditch. A Chester correspondent states that Mr. Gladstone is en- gaged revaluing the whole of the farm holdiogs on the Hawarden estate and, where the circums ances re- quired, considerable permanent reductions of rent have been made. NwivtLANcesifirtz JUSTICES.—On Friday morning Mr Henry D. Pickford, of Wrightingtm, Chorley ; Mr William Bryan, of Inca Hall, Wigan; and Mr Thomas Brocklebank, of Walton, Liverpool, were placed on the commission for the county of Lancaster; and Mr George Keighley, of Woodfield, Burnley, for the borough of Burnley. The announcement made in Parliament yesterday after- noon of the proclamation of the National League in Ireland, has caused intense excitement in political circles. A num- ber of Liberal members of Parliammt and of the representa- tive Liberals outside the House intend to proceed to Ireland to show their sympathy with the national cause. THE Cass CASE—The hearing of the charge against Con- stable Endacott of perjury in connection with the arrest of Miss Cass was resumed at Bow-street, on Friday. Sergeant Comber deposed to Endacott charging Miss Cass at the police station with soliciting in the public street. Other evidence having been given, Endicott was committed for trial, bail being accepted. , SINGULAR ACCIDENT —On Thursday a young man with one arm, n titled Joseph Johnson, was following his employ- ment at the Mowcroft Colliery, Bilston, when the hook attached to his artificial arm got entangled in the skip chain. lie WAS drawn nearly to the top of the pit, when the strap that held the artificial limb gave way, and he was rprecipitated to the bottom of the shaft, and death was in- stantaneous. A PLATELAYER KILLED.—A shocking' railway fatality happened at West Houghton, on Friday morning. A plate- layer named Adamson had just got his tools out of a cabin down the line, and was proceeding to his work, when a goods train approached. The weather was foggy, and in stepping out of the way, he got right in the path of another engine, was knocktd down, and his head laid open. Death was instantaneous. THE ECLIPSE OF THE SUN. A Berlin correspondent writes r During the eclipse of the sun on Friday morning the sky was entirely overcast, and the sun itself was not visible; the only thing observed was a deep colouring of clouds, which increased as the sun rose, and then gradually died away, whereupon a general increase of darkness sud- denly set in. After a few minutes the deep colouring of the clouds was again observed, and then dcylight ensued Man-, thousands of people repaired to various points of observation by train, in carriages, and on foot. THURSDAY NIGHT'S DIVISIONS. In the division on Thursday night on the motion that the Commons agree to the Lords' amendment to the Town .Parks Clause, the fol- lowing Maeral Unionists voted against the Government : Mr. Chamb•rlain ; Messrs. Heneage, Collings, Russell. Buchanan, Kendrick. Lea, Pitt-Lewis, Sinclair, and Powell- Williams, and one Conservative, Sir Charles Lewis. In the division on the motion to agree to the Lords' amendment to the Rent Revision Clause, Messrs. J. Chamberlain. Collings, Be ehanan, Russell, Kendrick, Lail, Pitt-Lewis, Sinclair, T. Sutherland, and Powell-Williams voted against the Govern- ment. _

div.head: DRIVER.
div.p: DRIVER.

An engine-driver nam:d—Alf-Q. Ling. of 98, Douglas- Street, Derby, who took a prominent part in the recent strike on the Midland Railway. on Friday; morning drowned his three children in the canal, and afterwards committed sui- cide by drowning hiniself. A number of papers relating to the strike were fouid on the deceased's body. He had applied for reinstatement, but all the vacancies had been filled, and the rssibility of no employment affected hie mind.
la INMAN LINER BURNT AT BEA.-THIRTEEN
LIVES LOST.

A Queenstown correspondent telegraph's that the steamer York City, from Baltimore, arrived off the Old Head of Kin- isle at eleven o'clock on Friday morning with the crew and passengers of the Inman line atamer City of Montreul on board. She signalled that the City of Montreal was burnt at sea. Tugs went Off to meet the York City. , Lloyd's agent at Queenstown telegraphs also announcing the arrival of the survivors of the City of Montreal, and I adds that 13 lives were lost in the disaiter. The City of Montreal left Naw York on the 6th August with 135 pas- sengers for Queenstown and Liverpool.

_ A London correspondent says that up to three o'clock on Friday afternoon no further details had been received of the burning of the City of Montreal, but the steamer York City, with the survivors, was expected to reach Queenstown harbour at that hour.

A later daspatch from Queenstown says the steam tender from the York City had returned bringing most of the passengers of the City of Montreal to Queenstown. They state that the Montreal took fire on the 11th instant. One boat containing seven of the crew and six passengers is missing. [UNDERWRITERS' TELEGRAM.] The fire was discovered on the 10th in toe after main or top deck. Fire hoses were pat on immediately, every exer- tion available, and appliances, includim; hand grenades, by the entire crew, and, passengers assisting. succeeded par- tially ; but matters being serious steered for St. John's Newfoundland. expecting assistance from passing steamers. At six next morning a fierce fire burst out in the forward after batch, and continued endeavours to extinguish it were without success. Seeing the ship was doomed, all beats
UG

were got nut, having been previously provisioned and prepared. The ship was left in flames from the main hatch aft at ten am., and remained near the burning ship. keeping the boats' heads to the heavy sea running until rescued by the German barque Trebant, except No. 8 boat. with thirteen on board, which was last seen running before the wind from the burning ship. We were transferred to the steamer York City on the following morning, and after searching for the missing boat without success, and the barque having promised to continue the search, proceeded for Queenstown, where all were safely landed.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at four o'clock,

—.— THE PROCLAMATION OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE.—TIie Marquis of SALISBURY said the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, by the advice of the Privy Council, bad to-day proclaimed the National League a dangerous association, under sec. 6 of the Crigies Act. Power bad thus been taken under that statute to prohibit and suppress that association in any dis- trict where such a step might be required to prevent intimidation or interference with the administration of the law.—The Trustees' Savings Bank, Public Works, Loans, and Friendly Societies Bills were read a second time. Tbe Commons disagreement to the Lords amendment in the Irish Land Bill was agreed to without discussion.
The House adjourned until Tuesday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Tbe House met at four o'clock.

THE WEN LAND BILL.—The Attorney-General for Ire- land brought up the Commons' reasons for disagreeing to the Lend Law (Ireland) Bill. Mr. T. Russell gave notice that early next session he should ask leave to bring in a bill to prevent the owners of town parks in Ireland appro- priating the occupiers' property therein. ARABI PACEIA Sir J. A. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Trevelyan, said he could not hold out any hope of the Go- vernment urging on the Egyptian Government the advis- ability of granting amnesty to Arabi Pacha and other Egyptian exiles. THE LIPSIII CASE.—The HOME SECRETARY, replying to Mr- Graham, said full facilities were given to Mr. Hayward to see the phial produced at Lipski's trial. He could hold out no hope of the respite of the unfortunate man being fur- ther extended. TILE NAIIONAL LEAGUE PROCLAIMED. Mr. W. JonersroN asked if it was true that the National League had been proclaimed P—Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland bad to-day proclaimed the Na- tional League as a dangerous association under the sixth section of tbe Crimes Act, and he had thus taken power to proclaim and suppress the League in any district where it interfered with the administration of the law. He had now

laid the proclamation on the table, and Thursday would be fixed to discuss the subject, if so desired.—Mr. W. o'.l3nrEar asked if it was known that the work of the National League was now principally confined to work of registration ?—dr. A. BALFOUR said the action of the League, as regarded re- gistration, would not be interfered with.—The announce- ment of the Chief Secretary for Ireland produced great excitement and disapprobation amongst the Parnellite mem- bers. LABOURERS' ALLOTMENTS.— [he House went into Com- mittee on the Labeirers' Allotment RITCHIE stated the result of the consideration by the Government or the amendments which stood on the paper. They had al- ready announced their willingness to accept any proposal, from whatever quarter it came, which would make the Bill more effectual for carrying out the object of providing means by which labourers throughout the country might be able to obtain allotments. After cansideration, they did not propose to adhere to provisions which set up quarter sessions as the tribunal to which ap- plication was to be made for issuing provisional orders in the event of Parliamentary powers being required for purchase of land. It was intended to accept an amend- ment which provided that, on the representation of not less than six Parliamentary electors of any parish, or distrie, it should be the duty of the Sanitary Authority to tike into consideration the desire at the labourers to have allotments. The managers at the allotments were, as the bill stood, to be appointed by the Sanitary Authority in both urban and rural districts, but it was pro- posed that, where representation was made, by a certain number of electors, and they desired to elect their own local managers ; and elections had to title place and should be conducted upon the principle of each man having one vote. It was also proposed to authorise in cer- tain cases to provide, where practicable, a sufficient fund to meet the demand for common pasturage. It was also pro- posed to allow greenhouses, tool houses, pigstye, and fowl houses on the allotments, provided that at the expiration of the tenancy, neither the sanitary authority nor the incoming tenant should be bound to take the buildings at a valuation.- Mr. STAVELY HILL proposed to amend the first clause, which gives a short title to the Act, by adding the words Is it providing that the Act and the Friendly So- cieties Act (1875) should be read and construed as one act. —Mr. JEss4 COLLINGS appealed to the hon. member to withdraw the amendment —Mr. J. CHAMBERLAIN also ob- jected to the proposal of Mr. Stavely Hill.—After discus- sion the amendment was rejected by 200 to 78.—0 n clause 2, which provided it to be the duty of the Sanitary Autho- rity to acquire land for allotment being pro- posed, Mr. RITCHIE moved an aineadment providing that the machinery of the Bill should be be put in operation by six registered Parliamentary electors. —Sir Wm. HARCOURT suggested the substitution of "rate- payers" for 'registered electors."—The amendment as ' moved by Mr. Ritchie having been agreed to, Mr. BRAD* LAUGH Moved to amend the amendment and moved the in- sertion of toe words "persons of full age," in plea of ' "registered Parliamentary electors."—On a division the amendment was rejected by 166 to 112.—0 n the motion of Lord EBRINGTON, the words "or ratepayers" were inserted , after "registered electors." • Datrr SITTING. j

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

We are requested to state that in the case at Runcorn County Court, reported in our columns on the 6th inst un- der the beading "Threatened action for perjury," the ad- dress of the defendant, George Jackson, should be given as Ship-street, Newtown, Frodsham, and not Church-street, Frodsham. _ . .

SUDDEN DEATH AT KINGSLEY.—On Wednesday an in- quest was held by Mr. Churton at the house of Mr. H. Lewis, Castle Hill, Kingsley, touching the death of Ann Jones, 58, wife of Mr. Joseph Jones, labourer, Kingsley. On Tuesday evening the deceased was returning home from a neighbour's house, when she suddenly fell on the road. Assistance was at band, but life was found to be already extinct. A verdict of 6' Death from disease of the larlrt " was returned. DETERMINED SUICIDE AT KINGSLEY. On Wednesday evening Mr. Churton (county coroner), held an inquest at the house of Mr. H. Tewis, Castle Hill, Kingsley, concern- ing the tragic death of a young man named Frederick Lewis. It appears from the evidence of the father, that deceased had just returned home from Widnes, where he bad been working on Tuesday. He complained to his father of not feeling well. The father told him that be had better get his tea, and then left him for about half an hour. On returning he found that his son had left the house. He then went into the yard, and noticing one of the stable doors open he went in and found the deceased hanging by a rope. The body was in a half kneeling posture, with the feet on the floor. But it is thought that at first the de- ceased must have jumped off something. The rope was im- mediately cut, but life was found to be extinct. The jury returned a verdict of "suicide by strangulation, whilst the deceased was in a state of temporary insanity."
DEATH OF MR. H. S. HALL. J.P.
OF ST. HELENS AND WIDNES.

The announcement of the death of Mr Henry Samuel Hall, J.P., of St. Helens, ard partner in the firm of Messrs. Hall Bros. and Shaw, Widnes, which occurred at his residence,Windle Grange, St. Helens, about half-past seven on Thursday morning, occa- sioned a painful feeling throaghout the district in which the deceased gentleman was so well known and highly respected. For many years past Mr Hall has been one of the recognised public benefac- tors of St. Helens, and a readiness to assist in every cause for the benefit and improvement of the poor, or the support of local deserving institutions, was one of his characteristics. Though a Churchman, his generosity did not extend to those of his own belief alone, but his many acts of charity were dic- tated irrespective of either religious or political con- siderations. The deceased gentleman was the son of the late Rev. Samuel Hall, M.A. and J.P., vicar of Billinge, and after spending his early life at the vicarage, he removed to London, where he occupied the post of sub-manager of one of the London banks He re- mained there some years, and on his return to St. Helens he was married, about 28 years ago, to Miss Catherine Cross, youngest daughter of Mr. John Ctoss, of Windle Grange, and he afterwards lived at that hall up to the time of his death. His widow survives him, but there are no children of the mar- riage. The deceased gentleman resided just outside the borough boundaries of St. Helens, and though he never took an active interest in the town's mu- nicipal affairs he manifested a keen interest in re- ligious and charitable matters. He was a regular subscriber and contributor to local institutions, and was a trustee in connection with Bispham's charity, Windle Dole Charity. &c. He was both a borough and county magistrate, and was raised to the Bench in 1868. For several years he has also been one of the visiting justices for the Rainhill County Asy- lum. He was a regular and consistent churchman, and a strong Lily-ral in his political opinions. Mr. Hall had been in a decliiong strte of health for some few years, and at various times had been under the attentions of Dr. Dahon, of Llandudno, where the deceased gentleman resided for a few months each year; Dr. Glynn, of Liverpool, and Drs. Gaskell and Twyford, of St. Helens. In June last he returned from Llandudno to his St. Helens residence and serious symptoms began to manifest I themselves. Heart disease, from which he had suf- fered, became complicated with other complaints, , and notwithstanding the utmost medical skill he

gradually grew worse, and expired at his residence, as stated, on Thursday morning at the age of 65 years. His remains will be interred in a new family vault at St. Helens cemetery on Tuesday next, and Messrs. J. W. and C. Marsh, undertakers, St. Helens have been entrusted with the arrangements. MAGISTeRIAL REFERENCEB. . _

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Mr. J. C. Gam- ble, who presided, announced with great sorrow the death of Mr. Hall. He was a most active magistrate, and a kindly and energetic man in all his private and business relations, and he was sure that all who had come in contact with him would regret his decease.—Mr. W. T. Husband. solicitor, remarked that since he came to Widnes about 10 years ago Mr. Hall had sat on the Widnes Bench, and it was with feelings of very great regret that he new heard of his death. In his capacity as magistrate I Mr. Hall had the respect of the whole inhabitants, and par- ticularly of the gentlemen who had appeared in court before him.—Mr. Knowles said during the few years he had prac- tised in that court he never met a more kind, a more cour- teous and a more considerate magistrate on the Bench, and he felt deeply sorry to bear of his death.—Mr. Barker. as superintendent of police at Widnes for several years also expressed his sorrow at the sid news. Upon taking his seat on the bench at St. Helens, on Thursday morning, Alderman Harrison, who appeared to be much affected, said that before the ordinary business of the court If as proceeded with be felt it his duty to refer to the loss which the bench had sustained in the death of their friend and magistrate, Mr. H. S. Hall. He was a magistrate many years before the borough bench was formed, and he had always given great attention to the business of the court. He was sure he was speaking the mind of all the magistrates at- tached to that court in saving how deeply his loss would be felt, and not only by his family, hot by the poor of the neighbourhood, to whom he was always a friend and bene- factor. He was sure he was speaking for every other gentleman in the town in expressing deep sympathy for Mrs Hall in the loss she sustained.

A WIDNES DISTRAINT CASE: SEQUEL TO 'FAMILY DIFFERENCES." Before His Honour Judge Thompeon and a special jury at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, an extra- ordinary case, arising out of " family differences," was in- vestigated. The plaintiff was Sarah Hallet, wife of George Hallett, of Widnes, and she claimed the sum of £25 from Hugh Stubbs, of Manchester, and Edward Manley, of Wid- nee, as agent for the said Mr. Stubbs, and she further claimed a sum of £25 from her husbend George Hallet. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared fee the plaintiff, and Mr. Edge. bar- rister, Manchester (instructed by Messrs. Diggle and Ogden, Manchester), defended Stubbs and Manley, while Hallet appeared on his own behalf.—Mr. Riley stated that the, plaintiff married the defendant Hallett on the 27th August 1877, after the passing of the Married Women's Property Act, which might have some effect on the law of the case. ' At the time of her marriage the plaintiff was, and still is the administratrix of the estate of a former husband, one Samuel Wyndham Daw, deceased. As the administratrix of her former husband's property and otherwise was pos- sessed of certain household furniture and effects which did not pass to her second husband by the act of marriage. Since her second marriage she had purchased other articles out of monies left by her late husband, and separate monies earned by herself as a dressmaker. On the 2nd May last the de- fendants Stubbs and Martley wrongfully seized and carried away the whole of the furniture, valued at about £5O, for arrears of rent alleged to be owing to Stubbs; and they subsequently sold and disposed of a portion of her property, refusing to return the remoiroder, which they handed to her husband, who was now in possession of them, and wrong- fully detained them. She now claimed compensation from the defendants for the loss she had sustained. ' Mr. Riley added that when the plaintiff mar- ' teed Hallett she had a nice house of furniture and had a slim of money in the bank. In the beginning of May last, Mr. and Mrs Hallett were living at 1, Mospratt-street, Widnes, which had shortly before been purchased by Mr. Stubbs, from the former owner. There were certain arrears owing to the former owner, but the sale of a house cinferred no right of distress upon a new owner. Mr. and Mrs Hallett had a disagreement, and Mrs Hallett fearing that the home might be recklessly broken up by her husband, wrote a letter to Mr. Martlev, stating that her husband George was "on his old games again," and she would rather the things went for an honest debt than that they should be dispersed by him. Directly afterwards the bailiffs came with an execution, and Mrs Hallett poin- ted out what things belonged to her, but all the things were takes, one of the bailiffs, named Reynolds, saying what be. longed to her would be sent bock again is the evening. A sale subsequently took place, but the plaintiff had never re- ceived any of her things or the proceeds of the sale handed over to her.—The plaintiff. Sarah Hallett, was then called. She gave evidence in corroboration of Mr. ktiley's opening statement, and stated that before she and her husband lived in Widnes they lived in Dorset, where there was a dispute between them, and they separated. The furniture for the house at Widnes was bought by her, with the exception of a few small articles.—During the ex- amination of the plaintiff by Mr. Riley, his Honour said it was a case which really ought to be settled privately. The whole matter had arisen through Mrs. Hallett writing the letter to Mr. Martley asking them to come and take the goods.—Mr. Edge said his clients would be quite willing to accept the payment of the legal debt in settlement.—Mr. Riley said Mr. Edge and his clients were certainly between two fires—the plaintiff and her husband.—Mr. Edge sug- gested that her clients should ha paid the amount of the arrears for relit, and that the question of the ownership of the goods between Mr. and Mrs. Hallett be referred for settlement to the Registrar.—After some further conversa- tion his Honour retired to an ante-room with Mr. Edge, Mr. Riley, and the plaintiff, and on their return into c, urt it was stated that no settlement had been come to. and the case was ultimately adjourned until the 12th October.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meeting of tl..e Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whistoo, on Thursday afternoon. There were present Mr J Fisher (chairman), Rev Dean Finegan, Messrs J Jackson, T Eatock, J Bnrchall, J Kenwright, C B Johnson, W Tyrer, B Syrler, W B Longton, J Buckley, J M usson, J Ranson, P Longton, J Whalley, W Gerrard, J W Wareing, J Ellison, E. A. Graves, J Griffiths, W Middieburst, J Lowe, and S ii Hartley (clerk). RELIEF—The Workhouse Mmter reported that there were 462 inmates of the house this week, 470 last week, and 471 in the corresponding week last year. THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND A Doc; BITE.—The Work- house Master reported that a man named William Hancox. a vagrant who was in the house, had been bitten by a mad dog, and the medical officer in his remarks reccmmended that the man should be sent to M. Pasteur, at Paris.—The Clerk explained that the Man was passing through Bainhill, and called at a farm house begging, when the dog in the yard attacked him. There was no evidence that the dog was suffering from rabies —ln reply to Mr. Middlehurst, the clerk stated that Dr. Hall was treating the man in the usual way.—Mr Johnson remarked that the doctor did not give any reason why he recommended the man should be sent to M. Pasteur.—The Rev. Dean Finegan said the most unfortunate part of the business was that they had no evidence at all whether the dog was affected or not. After some further conversation Mr. Johnson moved, and the Rey. Dean Finegan seconded that a messenger be sent to the farm where the man was bitten and that Dr. Hall be sent for to attend the Board meeting.—lt was subsequently ascertained that the dog be- longed to a Mr. Glover, farmer, near Bold, and it woald take a messenger two hours to go there and back to the work. house, and Dr. Hall was away from home.—The Rev. Dean Finegan then moved that the clerk and a veterinary surgeon should visit the farm, and if it was found that the dog was suffering from rabies that arrangements be made for the man Hancox to be taken over to M. Pasteur. He (the Rev. Dean Finegan) thought Dr. Hall had been remiss in his ditties in not giving the Guardians more explicit reasons why the man should be sent to Paris.—Mr. Wareing secon- ded the motion, which was adopted. THE WORKHOUSE Maxaamarm—The Clerk reported the receipt of a report by Mr. Cleator, one of the Govern- ment Commissioners under the Lunacy Laws, giving an excellent account of the manner in which the Workhouse was conducted with regard to the housing of the inmates and their condition. He recommended that in the male ward a few hammock beds should be put up.—Several Guardians considered the report a most satisfactory one, and it reflected great credit upon the management. THE WORKHOUSE .ALTERATIONS.—The minutes of the Building Committee showed that the architect, Mr. Gandy, had prepared plans showing accommodation for the females and the conversion of the front part of the house. The committee approved of the plan, and instructed Mr. Gandy to duplicate it on the male side of the, house. At an ad- journed meeting Mr. Gandy submitted such plans, and they were approved.—The minutes of the committee were confirmed, and it was agreed that the plans should be sent to the Local Government Board for approval. A NEW MEMBER.—The Clerk submitted the nomination papers and the certificate of the election of a guardian for the township of Rainhill. Mr. Joseph Musson, of Fair View West. Rainhill, was the only gentleman nominated, and he was declared duly elected on the 12th inst.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTawicu DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN,ThCI lions victory won for Gladstone and the Liberal party at this election will carry joy into thou- sands of Irish homes, and it will gladden the stout heart of our brave old leader, You represent millions of your fellow-countrymea, who, twelve months ago, were in <l. übt as to the v. isdom of the policy of entrusting to the Irish people the management of their own affairs, and of making them respnsible for good order in their own country. Your example will be followed hereafter on many a hard- fought field, and your victory to-day will Quicken our onward march to many another. It will bring to a speedy end the Infamous policy of Coercion, and usher in the dawn of a brighter day. You have cast aside once and for ever the fear that the new development of the old policy of trust in the people will result in disunion, You have for the first time seen clearly the utter failure of your well.meant attempts to govern Irtland against the will of the vast majority of her people. Your hearts have beenstirred to t heir depths by the sad story of Gleubeigh and Bodyke. and you have realised to the full the truth that the misery and the faults of the people of Ireland are In the main but the natural tesult of the system of law which has been forced upon them by your power. You have shown, too, how clearly you aow see that the spirit which to-day impels the Liberal party to demand Home Rule for Ireland is the same spirit which, in times g )ne by. has won so many fights for liberty in England. You have. righteously conclunned the cowardly slanders heaped upon the Roman Catholics of Ireland, and upon Mr. Parnell and his party in the House of Commons. You have heard the gospel of hate and you have not hearkened. Your vote Is an emphatic tepudiation of the claim of a few families still to monopolise the representation of Cheshire. You have shown again to-day what has been shown on so many a page of your history, that the people of this land are a great-hearted, a generous, a proud, and an independent people. For the honour done to me and for the trust reposed In me lam heartily grateful to the 5412 men who have recorded their votes in my favour. Espeolally do .1 value the services of the splendid band of volunteer workers who assembled early on Saturday morning In the Liberal Committee Rooms, to perform so memorable a day's work. To my gallant opponent, to his supporters, and to all, both men and women, are due my sincere thanks for the courtesy and good humour with which the contest has been waged. I remain, gentlemen, ' Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINOON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall, lforthwleh, August 15th, 1881.

SARAH BERNHARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND PATTI'S PERIL Sarah Bernhardt's receipts, for her late tour in South America, are the largest ever taken by any dramatic artiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spare! Patti has also achieved great success, and a very large amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came very near being the victim of a dynamiter who attempted to threw an explosive bomb at her while she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Francisco, California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a man in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from ander the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it. when it exploded In his hand, shattering his arm and face, and inflicting other injuries. Had the man not placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met biro an be was rushing down stairs, he would have been torn in pieces by the in- furiated people. Patti displayed great coolness and pres- ence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by singing "Home, Sweet Home." Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn gray through fright. Think of Patti with gray hair! A beautiful head of hair is the crowning glory of woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a rais- fortune which may be prevented by the use of that famous , hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent baldness and restore gray hair to its natural color, strength and gloss. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the civilized world.
